div.p: .1 THE VOLUNTEER FORCES OF THE UNITED KINGDON.

THE Statistical Returns of the Volunteer Forces I in the United Kiogdom for the year 1879 have been , pablinhed this week. The statement has a special I significance at this date, for it represents the numeri.l strength and the efficiency of our Volun- teer Army after the lapse of just twenty years since the Volunteer Movement WllB started. It was in the latter non' he of 1899, and the early months of IWO), that the first Volunteer Corps in this Citiren army were organised and officered, and the returns now homed relate to the position of these Forces on the 3lst of October, 1879. The movement had its rise in the public apprehension of the possibility of a French invasion, excited by the bluntering threats of certain colonels in the army of the French Empire under the third Napoleon. In that regard it Woo a repetition of the history of that earlier Volunteer movement which began about the year 1796, and in a few months assumed immense proportion., which was likewise caused by the conviction that the first Napoleon deakried to invade England if he could ace a chance lof doing no when the country W.lB unprepared. But I that former muster of Volunteer, for the defence of I the realm, enormous as it grew during the crisis of : the struggle with Bonaparte, had no permanence. Towards the end of the year DIG it became apparent that Napoleon's army encamped at Boulogne would I not attempt to crow the English channel, but was to I be employed in a campaign in Germany, and there- upon a good many of the Volunteer Corps which had been called into existenee were at once disbanded. inn short time the whole of the Voluntesr Forces of that period had vanistwd as completely as the base- less fabric of a dream, which leaves no wrack behind. How different has been the course thus far of the Volunteer Movement started in 1839180. The idea of a French invwsion of these ehores has long since ceased to be credible. The French empire itself hue again been swept away, and the bellicose colonels have go. wi th it. Nevertheless,theVultin teer Corps founded twenty years ago continue to exist and even to in- crease. The Volunteer Forces have become consoli- dated nun permanent portion of the defensive military eetablish meat of the nation. Nob,sly is heard to propose that a force 80 large, yet to cheaply kept up, ahould be dispensed with. Few of those who volun- teered twenty years back can yet be in the ranks; but as the elder men retire the younger men step into their places. The popularity of Volunteering has not declined with the mamaoe of its novelty. At the end of last October, the establishment consisted of 200,230 men of all arms enrolled; and of 197,485 men returned an efficient. The increase on the total of the preceding year is more than :1,000 men. The , small balance of non-efficierrts has diminished from 9,022 in 1678 to 8,7115 in 1879. In the table of the official return we find with a degree of pride, as Lan- cashire men, that the body of Vol unteere enrolled In Lancashire remains some thousands larger than are enrolled in any other County of England or of Scot- land. The total number of Lancrwhire Volunteers Is 25,513, and no fewer than 23,115 of them are ern- ciente. Middlesex comer, woad with 17,001) Volun- teers, Yorkehire COLOtia third with 13,034 Volunteers, Lanarkshire, in Scotland, which includes the great city of Glasgow, comes Munh on the list with 10,180 Volunteers; and the three next counties are Surrey, Cheshire, and Durham, which have each of them be- tween 5,000 and 5,500 Volunteers. Laneitobire, which is first in this department of patriotic service, and maintains an Army of Volunteers as large as the British section of the Allied Armies which fought and conquered at Waterloo, has, to be sure, the largest population of ail the counties But we have made oats little table which ahows that among the English counties we have named as furnishing the largest contingents to the Volunteer Force, Lanca- shire and the adjacent County of Cheehire have also the largest number in proportion to population, and are only excelled by the Scottish County of Lanark, which taken the premier place M this proportional enrolment of volunteer soldiers. The comparison is presented in the etatement below, which gives the population of each county at the census of 1871: Population noel Proportion to County. in /871. V1A1111.15. Population. Lannaihire Iduldlefsz Yorkshire 2444,710 ... 13034 .... 1 lo 187 Ltnneltenire 705,279 ... 10,184 ... ifs 78 13orrify Chsablfs 4 539,785 ... 5,215 ... ifs 104 Um Wu Gera we see the relative amounts of Volunteering for unpaid military service which have been supplied by the principal metropolitan and oommencial, manu- facturing, or mining population centres in England and ileottrnd. Litharkshire has one Volunteer for every 11l inhabitance ; Cheshire has one in 1114; Lan- cashire has one Volunteer to every 112 inhabitants; and Durham, Middlesex, Yorkshire, and Surrey fol- low in order. These seven Counties together furnish not far from one-half of the entire Volunteer Forces of the country, whilst their united population is about one-third of the population of the United Kingdom. Some of the agricultural counties in England which yield the smaller numbers and pro- portions of Volunteers are these,— ' -4 P.roposifon to

Upon the whole, the Volunteer Forses am dietributed pretty equally over the coun- try, and there Is not much room for the inference that the martial spirit, or shall 'recall it the patriotic impulee to help in the defence of the country in case of need, permeates the population of some provinces oi the Kingdom more than others,

Saturday's Tinto say.:—When Mr. Bright turns from domestic affaita to the aspect of our foreign and colonial relations he is more animated, but less convincing. No humane man can pretend not to be shocked by the contempla- tion of the lioT rors of war. No right.thi Acing man would attempt to defend a war demonstrably unjust. But Mr. Bright's denunciation of the horrors of all wars and the wickedness of unjust wars is vitiated at the outset by his sweeping declaration that he believes all were to be savage and cruel. If we are not mistaken. we have heard • differ- ent, a more temperate, hut not quite so pacific,s, strain even from Mr. Bright himself, while the war in the United States was in progress. The cruelty of war does and should make on hesitate to engage in it save as a painful duty, and in obedience to Metice and necmsity, but it does not in itself effect the question of i. jostice.. Nevertheless', it is not amiss that we who, as Mr. Bright says, live in peace. 30 far away teem all the horrors that war entails, should be re- minded of the responsibility we undertake when we sanction • war, even with a full conviction of i. necessity. But Mr. Bright's voice would be still more pereuasire and con. conning than it is if he would be content to tell us what war , costs in suffering and sorrow without asking kis to believe that the principles which we all profess and strive to follow condemn it altogether.

AFOttAT • A corresponti.nt of the Pail,' „Vet, stius that the condi- tion of the trans,' t service 151 Afghani,rit M most die- . graceful. Not long since the department managed to get Welber 6,000 ponies at Jhelum, but one-third of Mem were unfit for use, as being either two young or too old, or two weedy or woithlesa on account of nom Wan.. Still, many at those which were retained were undoes ; and the corres- pondent adds "The Government are entitled to our v•iiii•the and likely en ogh they would have it if only they were honest, which they are not and had the moral courage,. which they never have, to forlsnat from virtually claasaymg as transport animals wretche I beaeta tit only for the knackeen yen,. Many of Otero have literally been gar red on the wsv down from Cabot, and yet the Military Department assurr. us that euoplies are plentifol all along the line. I affirm it, and the thing can be [proved, that the mortality among them animals has been caused jug as much y etteer hunger as lue hard work and clumsy handling." A telegrain from (Sabot gives currency to a rumour that figoub Khan, Yakoob's elder brother, is making hie way from Herat to Klutente, and that be will .15ortly arrive at that place and join Mahound Jan in an expedition against Cabul. Thn Daily Yb e correspondent at Cobol telegraphs that, nothwithstanding that li.eral Roberts is doing all lie can to reassure the iolmbitants of that Gwital by occupying the Bala Hismr, constructing military roads around the city, and building gone piquet towers on the heights on both sides of the now falcona gorge, the llindoo tamitie.. who form the most industrious portions of the cite, are migra- ting in loge numbers to Iteshawur for fear of the return of Mahomed Jan's forces. Mahomed Jan is reported to have homed a proclamation to the Afghane, in which he announced his ietermination to renew, on thellth February, his attack on the British force • at Cabul. The Kohistanis are preparing an expedition to co-operate with Mallomed Jan. TURKEY. Sir Ifenry Lavard ban decided not to reply to the last despatch tithe Ottoman Foreign Minister defending the course taken by the Porte onto the minsionary incident. He acknowledges the good intentions of the Porte in the matter, and thinks there is no occasion to re-open the discussion. The convention which hts jug been signed by the Ottoman Foreign Minister and Sir Henry Layard, on the part of their respective Governments, to suppress the slave trade in the Sultan's dominions, given England aright of search on board vessels flying the Turkish flag, and provides that slaves may be taken from ships inrthich they may be found. ITALY. I. .

The Wing of Italy has signed a decree proroguing the Italian Parliament. A correspondent of the hail g :Nit, at Naples, writes on the 21st A strange and horrible murder was committed here last Sunday. A man of humble position in life, named Domenico Ippolito, fifty yeam of age, who lived with his wife in a poor rootn in the disused monastery of St Thotnas d'Aquino, lay dying of inflammation of the lungs. The doctors had given him up, and the heat consolations of re- ligion had been administered. About three o'clock on Sun- day afternoon some neighbour, heard a shriek from the room of the sick man, and Imlieved it to proceed from his "rife at the death of her husband ; Ind immediately afterwards the door of the room opened, and the wife rushed out, exclaim- ing 'Madonna! One of her neighbourn ran to the dying man to inquire the cause of the wound, when he with difficulty pronounced the word, 'Sire robbed moot my two francs and I have done for her.' The woman died immediately after being taken to the hospital, and her mur- derer, who was elan removed to another hospital and inter- rogated by the alithOlitieS, had net strength to tell them his name, when i.e too succumbed to his malady. Groanos Wtfinvighn. released front duty with the army of occupation in Prance, having in his pocket a con- siderable sum of arrears of pay and a long leave, sot in tle dull wainscoted coffee rooms of an hotel in the neighbom. hood of Piccadilly, where the Dover coach had deposited hien. Hard service had seasoned the boyish beauty of the 1 face which had I.ked love into the eves of JenriY lane and defiance into those of her father. It had not worn Idle as it had Oliver North. He looked strong and full of health, his fair complexion reddened by exposure to the weather, and the h.t of the sun, his broad chest more expaushee than ever, his limbs cleanly cut and firmly knit. I He wore his moustache, which drooped luxuriantly over his ' full red lips. A man now full grown, George was not altered except in this. A picture of robust youth when he drew his sword to march with his company that autumn morning in the old Derbyshire market place, he was now Gat sons picture finished,developed .to manhood. In his loose negl egi undress uniform, people turned to look at hirn in the london streets; for h • had been in town some weeks, having important financial business to settle with the War Office and other duties belonging to the close of a long and important military service. Al Dover he bad sat down and composed a long and serious letter to his father, asking to be received at the Vicarage as of old with open arms, begging his father to let bygones be bygones. "I deeply regret and deplore the past, sir," be wrote, "and would atone to the full ill knew how. I trust that on honeet endeavours to carry the family natne unsullied through the dangers of a great war has in a measure removed from your mind the recollection of the folly of my 'moth it has been a source of continual repr.et tore,, when I have looked back ; and I ahould have suffered beyond endurance, hod I not felt that in your heart you could not hold me in continual abhorrence and had I not also have been equally assured of my mother's prayers." Then be referred to the pleasant days of his boy- hood, to his father's great charges in respect of his educa- tion, thanking the Vicar for all this .d for his noble example of courage and rectitude, and concleded by aaying, "it one regret more *than having parted from you in anger hos troubled toe, it has been that I did not obey your com- mand and rnarry as yon wished. That poor loving girl has been ever in my mind, and I never considered that I esteemed lier sufficient to make her my wife fintil I was far beyond reach of her. I trust, sir, you have been a father to her, an you declared you would be, and that it is well with her, for great was her trouble, and sore hir need. God forgive me for it. Touching what passed between myself and Miss Manners, I leave that to be ordered as yea may think best for her happinene and your own honour.' It was an honest, manly letter, the work of one who bad been tried, who bad been face to face with death many a time, who had looked en ',cones of slaughter and misery, who had witnessed acts of heroism in men as well as in women, who had seen wonders of devotion and self-sacrifice among the daughters of Spain and France, and who had learnt higher and nobler lessons from war than most men who had fought their way from Madrid to Vittoria, from Vittoria to Waterloo, front Water!. to Paris. George's was a sociable nature, and when he left home the lad did not know how home memories would cling to him, how Ilia heart would go hack to the Vicarage to his father and mother and to that unsophisticated, unthinking girl, with her musical Scotch accent and her soft winning ways. He thought him- ae:f 0 "devil of a fellow," a sort of Capt. Plume, a lady-killer, a lad of mettle, a soldier who was geing forth to tnake con- quest of hearts, as well as of forts and fields, a Don Juan and a Hector in on, instead of which he bad gradually dis- covered that he war just an average honest, thoughtless, brave young Englistonan, with, on the whole, more than an average sense of his moral and religious responsibilitiee ; and what m more, that instead of his having made a conquest of the pretty little lassie at the Post-office under the shadow of the crooked spire she had made a conquest of hint. He had lain many a night thinking of her and almost cursing him- self that le bad not marred her. Duncan Macfarlane, the hare mention of whose name aS a sort of relation bad turned his stomach in that last interview with his father, had long since ceased to be regarded except with the respect due to the father of the girl he really loved George was changed indeed, and yet he might have argued that he hail not changed at all ; that hewn, a raw, inexperienced, selfish youth at Chesterfield, since which time the innate good in him had come out, bad developed, had grown with his manhood, to the necessary annihilation of those vicious qualities which be had in hie greenness imagined worthy and manly. Ache had neared the white dills of Albion his longing to sec Jennie again had taken hold of him with increasing power. "I am cotning back, my own little Jennie, I told you I should," he had written Lefore embarking at Calais, "and you will find toe, though now a Major— meek you, a Major, Jennie—still the same old affectionate George." He had asked his father to reply to the hotel at which he should stay in London, and the Vicar did to, but not until he had taken time to consider well what he should my, and his wife had agreed with him that the truth and the whole truth was Aiwa), beet at all times. Scithe Vicar had written as

"MvdoorSnn,—l°oeeo you are, George, and always have lane, notwithstanding the grief I did suffer under long and sore, and thy mother likewise. from thy &bland disobedience. That said, give me leave to confess thy letter has given me and tby worthy mother gred joy, and it hi a comfort to me Co feel that us a soldier you haveilone credit to the country Cleat bred you, and to the name you bear. You have done more than carry your sword with honour, my son—you have conquered yourself. Palitur qui rirreif But he becomes strong, and the truth will not be able to cant him down, for even acme sow shall we reap. Prepare then, to receive ill news with that which is good. As for me and thy nmther, we stretch our arms out to thee, and our free and full forgiveness goes to thee with this letter. Thy father's house is thy due resting-place, and the fatted cali shall be killed. . .

"Yet must the news hereof which thy mother thinketh with me proper for thee to know, be of sadness, since your letter speaks of Jennie Macfarlane, the mother of your chikl. God 18 good, met she way yet live; but four years and some weeks since sight of her or report of her have glad- dened Duncan or myself. Sore beset with the women of this town, who could not forgive her the sin thou hadst put upon her, she fled the virtuous furies, a plsgne upon them, and has been lost to es es if she had died. I fear me Duncan Macfarlane was hard upon Ile, in truth I know he was, and he has not prospered from sickness to drink and to the loss of his employment brought hire to the humble position of our gardener here at the Vicarage, but this day he is transferied tote friend's employment in the Peak, whither he goeth by the coach, as thy mother advised it were bmt he be not in the way when we welcome thee home.

• " Replying to thy enquiries as touching Miss Manners, she, with xnv full consent, married the Yorkshire baronet, who, for a time, was much concerned at the prospect of: being cast off by her. He is a good husband, she is a true : and happy wife, and they do live on his estate in the East I Riding of the great county of the North, and are likely to have numerous successors to their wealth. So may heaven prosper them in their love and estates. In which prayer it rejoiceth on to know thou wilt concur. " . . . . .
In Ihi letter there mingles no in life good and HI, joy and sorrow. Bear both as thou host borne thine honour in

the battle field, and come home n ith all speed to a father's heart and a mother's arms. And know, my son that thy mother hath recovered much of her former health, and doll] now share the exercise and delight of the household duties. charred. They have brought your letter addressed to Jennie to the Vicarage She was most unfortunate and . a . • . • • .
though happineSs in -marriage is found among equals of birth and station, it had pleased thee, Georen, to make her the equal. and it may be within theepossibility of thing. . . • • ' "

av equal, j that the report in the Gazettes and journals of your return may induce her, if she he living and in honour as I truly think if in life, to disclose her retreat and condition, and as Horace bath it—

He sat without moving for half-an-hour with i his father' letter in his band, and then be read it again and I again. The brave little heart, he thought, how it had gone , forth from the gruel place. He mold umlerstand how Jennie, in her tradeen way, had turned back on the canting byoo- critical town. What names he called it in hie silent agony and pardon sitting there in the unsympathetic coffee rOOM of the old tavern, forgetting for the moment that he had , been niece cruel than the town of his nativity. With what strange nensnions of fear and dread, of love and longing, he read that passage of hie father's nar. 71;ere was madness in the thought that his child might be living in poverty and wretchedness, its mother enduring unbend-of privations. lint there was a faint gleam of hope in this matlnnsa, which, however, only glimmered for a moment to fall dead at the suggestion that Jeanie no longer lived. lie gat amt thought of every conceivable thing she might have done, and his tnind wandered to Miller's Dale, the wayside inn, and the kindly landlady there. Thither he had advised her to go if she should not be well treated at home. 'rile only thought that gave him ace drop of comfort and patience was the remembrance that he had forced a sum of money upon her at parting. Yet surely intim search the Vicar would institute,the little fishing station on the Derby- shire Wye would not escape notice. Then again it might. 'file valets of Derb, shire were Icr. incognito to half Chester- field, and few persons came and went in that shady retreat whither Jennie, supposed to be on a viAt to relations Cu away, bad accompanied her lover one never-to-be-forgOttei happy summer. What would he now have given to recall it to blot it out, and to have left Jennie in her innocence at home or to have been ruled lay his father anal made her tit: VI.Cs daughter ! How generous, how Boole, he thought new was his father's conduct compared with his own, man proud of his blood, a soldier ouch high in command and now robe had once said, a soldier of Christ, he had deigned to goon even no low as to call Duncan Macfarlan brother ; yet had he, his degenerate son, thought it a An • • thing lo rave the poor pretty unselfuth girl and plume Id hit for other conquests, for fresh woods and pastures new! , George's love burned fiercur cow far the check it encoun- tered, and hie debasement, in his own estimatian, filled him COI a 1,14:3:11IP mad aMictirna of rename. I buckled on hie sword anti wont out. Waffiing is a re-' lief to an overwrought mind, and it helps a man to l'f ink. When a certain grnt author encountered his first great trouble isi life, lie started off and walked twenty tones with- out stopping. George Wingfield felt a similar itnpulse. Ile gratified it. At the aline time he resolved all manner of schemes or the diacovery of Jennie Macfarlane. Alive and still true to him, he would marry her. Dead. Le would lai, a monument to her. Ile hoped that she would 'ind in her child iD incentive to live, an inducement to obtain employ- ment, and also a comfort, he thought. Perhaps she had fallen into benevolent hands? Some kindly disposed lady had taken compeesion ..her. 0, if she were only aliveand well under 'fame hospitable roof, how he would reward her for her sufferings, how grateful he would be to her new friends! That ,mrinudgeon, her contemptible father, it was wise in the Vicar to send him away. The idea that she might Lave found an asylum M the Derbyshire valley near Buxton was dissipated on reflection, I;tit while to was walking and thinking he turned into the office of the Chief rd Police and consulted that astute official, who, after • I short enquiry connected with the detective department of ' the force, offered to send e messenger down into the country !,,,re he would et the present moment have the advice of pa lops the most capable officer in the service who was en. I o ;skin another matter on the spot. The suspicious death ' of the murder of Lord Ellethie on the doe of his marriage was news to George Wingfield, who had beard nothing of Oliver North for a long time except that he had been struck mit of the Army List, and the fact of Susan Ilardwicif's , marriage now convinced him that his brave comrade was indeed dead. This for the moment put aside hisown trouble. I Often all death was more dreadful than his own living son- , row. Though George had seen the grim monster in every shape, once outside the sweep of his darts he rejoiced in life. I lie was strong, full-blooded, of genial instincts, and he only scorned death when he was fighting his country's enemies. He eagerly engaged the services of the plice, and a mussel,- . ger was ordered to proceed to Chesterfield by the next coach, take counsel with Mr. Speller, make every enquiry as to Miss Macfarlane's disappearance, and report to London, meanwhile extending his personal enquiries to the neigh- bourhood of Miller's Dale and Buxton.

Conscious that he had taken the promptest and most available means of iretituting a search for Jennie and her child, he walked with a more hopeful and elastic tread, though Oliver North and Susan Hardwick ran gloomily M his thoughts. The suspicious death of Lord Ellerbie! Had Scruton succeeded then? He had not thought to aide the question. If that swashbuckling knave was now the Earl so much more the reason he thought for him to hate Cheeter. field and resolve not tn tévo there when he found Jennie. He knew nothing of tholluly reported death of Scruton, the epitaphs at Brackenbury and Chesterfield. No each good news as that entered into his hopes; for in his own ex- perience though death has the cnslit of being no respecter of persons, he had seen the hest fellows fall first. In all the eady battles of the Peninsula the young and brave and good comrades it seemed to him were invariably selected for the list of killed. It would be quite within *Lis view that Serrano should be alive and North dead, that he, liiinself, for that matter, should come home with only clew scratchea and a scalp wound or two, while Tom Bertram ehould have long weary spells in hospitals and lose en eye. "But give me the chance to atone,' he said to himself, "and I trill atone."

lie load scarcely given a thought shoat whither his steps were carrying him since he had retained the services of the police, though be had already excited some attention among the belles and exquisite, of the Park. Hts absent manner, his long 'winging etride, his stalwart figure and bronzed face, ed his generally unstudied, yet fine soldierly gait inade him quite a figure in the Park though he was in competition with the Persian Ambassador of the time who used to ride • white Arabian steed, gaily caparisoned, but not more showily arrayed than himself. Hietory repeats itself. One year it hi the kmbassador, with a fair Circassian in him train. whet excite. the nation of England to n wild pitch ot curiosity ; the century wanes and the Shah himself dazzles us with hie gem. and tires feminine curiosity not to say masculine envy with his trinity of veiled and therefore beautiful wives. Both the one and the other went home utterly stupefied with ' what they had seen, the laid visitor ntore bewildered than the other; for in lois notes on the envois of modern London the Shah explains that the police officere who administer end control the traffic are selected for their handsome figures from the upper classes, and that to insult one of them, the penalty is death. The past and the preeent are curiously linked in all departments of life. To-day in artistic Ureic. floe ladies are dressing very much after the fashion of the latter day. of the eighteenth century, which was the mode adopted by Susan Hardwick, Mary Kirk, anti Jennie Macfarlane at the

. . of the present history but they were necessarily behind the metropolis, and happily ao, for London had left off the short stayl. waist of Susan Hardwick in our first picture of that tantalising beauty under the elms by km father', door, and had revived that eyetem of tight lacing which obtains in the present day to the utter de.truction of health and beauty. The Park when Major Wingfield promenaded there with hie long stride and his thoughtful face was a picture of strange toted dresses, male and female, gro.sque poke bonnete, and tell strange hate, wasp waist!, and sandalled shoes: for men short blue coats,' tight trousers, narrow brimmed tall hats, cocked over the noee, but not eons to hide an oiled lovelock on the left temple. Our women show an inclination to follow the changes which began in 1700, when Paris adopted the sand-classic robes of Greece, and which by imitation and adaptat4n became in England the short-waisted, low-necked, short-sleeved cling- ing gown of an Englieb lady of fashion in the first days of the present century, and which governed country belles and county ladies long after the mode had clmoged into tight lacing and other extremes in the metropolis. Fashions wens slow to change in the country districts of our fathers, and Hardwicke, Kirk, Mrs. Kirk,the Vicar, and their families with slight modifications clung to the habits of dress and' manner which obtained in the days of Goldsmith and Dr. Johnson' ms ith the exception of that " baby-waist " gown' of Mies Hardwick, which ware slight advance on the time, attributable to Suean's occasional etudies of The Lady's Monthly Museum of the period. The country for many years was as little influenced by the vagaries of fashion in London as it was by the wicked stucco reign of Nash in the !natter of street and domeeticarchilecture ; and so if you would fully realise the day, in which this history moves, with the dresses of the period and rho bricks and tnotar of the time, you must fill your mind with reminiscences of the snug picturesque houses of the eighteenth century which Mr. Norman Shaw is reviving at Kensington, Hampstead, and in other directions; you must think of the old village greens and their fringes of ivy-coloured houses, with dia- mond window panes ; you must picture the market-places :I Nottinghern and Derby and Cheeterfleld with their Mona piazzas, their I, dr-windowed shopsond their canvas-covered stalls you most picture Derbyshire before railway twins, when .Buxton was in its infancy, when the roadside Mlle in the Peak were plain, comfortable looking lioness, often built of local stone quarried in the neighbourhood ; when a drive through the hillsand dales of the famous Midland county was free from the everlasting reek of the limekiln, the mea- dow blasting hand of the miner, and the screech of the loco- motive r and yet for all tide change you have only to look back from seventy to eighty years. In the matter of drens, you could hardly have any more picturesque guide than The Mad Dog illustrations of Caldecott, issued in the pre- sent year of grace nor could you have a better example of the education and art progress of these days than in a cum- parieon of the children's literature of now and then as ex- emplified in the toy-hooks of 1879 and those of 1800. And yet, strange to say, we have tolerated all these years the ghastliest change from the pictureeque to the ugly in the matter of architecture that ever afflicted a nation. It was said of a great Etnperor that he found Rome a city of stone and left inn city of marble, in reference to which it bar been said of Nash that he found London a city of brick and left it a city of etucco. Happily an old English revival has met in, and if you would try and recurs the rural and provincial England of these districts where local building done walnut abundant you have only in fancy to put Caldecott's men and womea into Sharer houses, reducing the ornamentation of the latter and toning down the colours with age, to find youreelf at home a hundred years and more ago while thinking of the scenes in which this present hietory passes you will scatter here and there the stone-built houses of the Peak with the red-tiled and the thatched buildings of Ches- terfield, the low straggling homestead. of Grassmoor, and the lichen-covered walls of Brackenbury. As for the justi- fithtion of the romance of our hietory, and what may he mini its improbabilities. the real story of the times gives ample warrant, the records of old families equally startling revelations, and the Newate Cnlenlar even sadder episodes than that of the Old Bridge Inn here set forth.

div.p: CONGREGATIONAL CILLTRCH, NORTHWICII FAREWELL SERMON.

On Sunday evening net the Rev. James Johns, RA., who for nineteen years has been the pastor of the Congregational Church, Northwich, preached his farewell sermon, in con- , sequence. of bin acceptance of a call to another church at Totnes, in Devonshire. The r,v. gentleman took his text from the 13t1t chapter of the Second Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians, at the llth verse : " Finally, brethren, fare- well. Be perfect, beat good comfort, he of one mind, live in peace and the God of love and peace shall be with you." Also from the let chapter of the Epistle of Paul to the Philippians. and at the Mb verse 'Only let your con- versation he as it becometh the Gospel of Christ : that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the Gospel." The rev. gentleman, in the course of his sermon, mid that there was a time when ministers had no longer to remain among the charges with which they had been identified, undo little change was desirable for themselves and congregation. A change was desirable to repair the health winch had been impaired, and fora congregation also to do more good than they had hitherto done. There were some people who listened to the mme voice fora good many years, and Rat in the same pew every Sunday; yet the voice of the preacher had lost aJI the interest and freshness that it once possessed. When a minister new anything of that kind, it he had any anxiety about the good of souls, he would at once seek to go where there was more interest in his labours, and where he might be a greater power of doing good. Even where that was not the case, where there Canon manifest waning of interest, a minister would often feel a doubt whether he ought to remain there. There were conscience, that he could not awtken, and hearta that he could not Mduce no love the Saviour ; and when that was the case it became a question with that minister whether it was not right kr him to move, and let mute other voice try to awaken thoae dead and careless. heart,. If at that moment there should be a call to some other field of labour, it Was an indication that it mete call from God bidding hint to go and work else- where. Re felt that God nos surely oulliog bin, Co premb the Gospel to those a Ito invited him. A time like that had come in leis (the preacher's) hidory. He had looked at the circumstances that surrounded him, his own health, and Choir spiritual condition, and, after great perplexity and great anxiety, it seemed to him right that lie should go else- where and try Cr do good in another region. and let some- one else take hi. place and preach the gospel of Christ with more enccese than he had been enabled to do. Ha lett that, in going torts new !tient, and see new fmres, he was doing it against his own e ill; Inn he had thonght it right to re- sign his pastorate, and, now that the last hour heel come. ho hoped he might speak m [limn word, that might be helpful to some in the future history of the church. Ile exhorted thew. to he perfect and of one mind, and to liye in peace. , Re had found them in peace when he came. and lie left three, in peace. If he thought that floe peace of the church would he disturbed he should be griPVQ4, because where peace was di,turbed prosperity was destroyea. After addreasing them very earnesrly on Cho noceasity of working together f,,r the 10,,1 of the chorch, the preacher concludod with ewes. elt.inent and toncbing valediction. An appropriate hymn was sung, and after prayer the large congregation dispersed.

GOSSIP FROM TIIE WORLD. "Atlas," in the World of IVedn— esday, has the following— hear on the best authority that there is no wound for the report, which has been widely circulated, with regard to a marriage between a noble lord and a young testesac the Strand Theatre. /3y the way, the lain in question is not "a professional dancer as well as actress," 0 has been stated by a contemporary. Madame Patti begins her performance at the Gait.; in Paris, not in the middle at February, as previously an- nouncid, but on February 4th. She 211 ti Nicolini receive a nightly silary of 1400 Her notary, lam told, paid her husband £40,000 to insure his non-interference. This is simply the story of Giulia (iris' and her husband over again. I bdieve that in the coming session the leaders of the Opposition will decline to afford the Governinent any assist- ance in dealing with the Obstruetives, or in forwarding the business of Parliament his not that the Liberal chiefs love the Oben-actives, but that they despise the present House of Commons : they think that it has outlived itstime, and that anything which tends to hasten its end is deserving at least of tacit support. Bishop Fraser and his bride are still at Torquay, staying quietly at the 13elgrave Hotel. Here they will remain for some ten days longer, and they will then proceed direct to Bishop's Court, Manchester. The Manchester people would be glad to give them an enthosi.tie welcome, but the Bishop is inexorable in his resolve that as little fuss as possible shall be made over his marriage. Nevertheless, it is understood that a large number of valuable prawn. are awaiting Mrs Fraser at the palace. The Admiralty is to be congratulated on its derision to send an ironclad turret-ship to Hong Kong. The one iron- clad already on the China station is not sufficient to insure the protect'ou of our immense interests in the far Kist. The growth of the Russian naval establishment et Vladivostock has always been kept in view by the Admiralty. no That muclnabused department is more fully alive to the naval requirements of the country than is generally sup. posed. Various matters are now leaking out which show hose Complete were the dispositions it bud made in case the Jingoes should lead us into war two years ago. Von Moltke himself could not have been more exact in providing for porsible contingencies. It has been stated in certain quartereihat the chiefs of the Opposition have made up their minds that a dissolution will take place before the first of May. The fact may have Name bearing upon this, that Mr. Lowe, who had privately agreed to take, early in the spring, a prominent part in a Liberal demonstration in an important city of the West, where the posit:on of parties is very nicely balancel. has suddenly "hanged his mind, and postponed his visit indefinitely.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JANUARY 31, 1180.
FARMERS ANL PINCHING TIMES.

ream speaking is invariably an accompaniment of pinching times. Agriculturists, hitherto pemusded that from successful farming and from teumt farmers' best interests roryism was inseparable, are beginning to discover that the party of "gunpowder and glory' is eelfish at the beet, and that its pretence to be the next best friend of tenant agriculturists is hollow and unreal. In what arecommonly called " piping time's" the bulk of Engliuhmen have a weakness for glitter, for displaying an air of superiority over the rest of creation, cod for exhibiting an indifference for " eheme•paring," just as if they had u guarantee . .

that the sun of prosperity, which enkindle in theme friskiness of spirit aud a disregard for trifin, would never sink beneath the commercial horizon. Ito then I that the " gunpowder anal glory" party, which dialikes to bother with " oandle ends" nod hates trifles, is in the ascendant; but as soon ais that party has emptied the national cask box filled by the mixings of the Liberals, as the result of a steady pursuit of a "cheese. poring' policy, and of their Laving taken caro of

" candle ends" and trifles; as soon as fire and sword have been carried into other nations and humanity outraged under the frivolous pretext of main- taining "prestige " ; as men as the march fur " glory" abroad by rubbery and murder under the name of " war " has reducesl our trade with foreigners and wrecked the businesses of home manufac- turera ; as soon as the game of "fireworks" has been well-nigh played out, the national debt increased, and the screw of taxation tightened so that the cost of the murderout "entertainment" may be met, then the "gunpowder and glory" party begin to mitt their adherents, and the " cheeseparing " party, which takes caro of "candle ends," and has regard for "trifles," again becomes paranount, and keeps to the surfaoe until " piping times" again return, when the "gunpowder and glory" party secures an innings which lasts until it has produced disccutent and distrust abroad, and by extravagance cleared out the national cash box and ruined the fortunes of thousands at home. And so in the whirligig of politics parties rise and fall. These party vicissitudes, however, are chiefly traceable to changes of opinion and action of voters in boroughs. Partly from fear, partly from an unexplainable belief in the wily professions of the squirearchy, which constitutes the forefront of the party of "gunpowder and glory," tenant farmers have hitherto been the mainstay of Toryism. The gloom which has swept over the commercial and manu- facturing communities consequent spin the "gun- powder and glory " policy of the Government, has extended to homesteads iu nearly every rural retreat, ats its depressing effects have been intensified by the disastrous failure of the harvests. The present, therefore, is ga "pinching time" for farmers, and their outspokenness manifests a discontent with those relations between landlord and tenant that the "gunpowder and glory" party have striven to per- suade them were pee treePenre. On Thursday, the members of the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture assembled at Crowe to discuss the question, introduced by Mr. Thomas Rigby, the Seem-; tarp, "Case Cheshire farming he better adapted to mitigate the effects of the present agricultural depres- ! sion, and to meet foreign competition in the future ?" Mr. Rigby, whose remarks we publish in another , column, took a common sense view of the ditticulties with which tenant farmers are beset. The picture he drew by no meant redounds to the credit of Toryism, which has all along assumed a sort of fatherly interest , in the affairs of farmers, but this has simply been amide to win popularity at the polling booths. There ' are Liberal leaders of to-day who, for fully a: third of • century, have contended against the per- petuation of the anomalies in the laud laws, and the unfair positions to which tenants were reduced by the ; arbitrary powers of owners of the soil. Allured at the time of elections by promisee, that were afterwards ignored, of the Tory party, agtioalturists continued I their allegiance to that party, and when the present Government rode iuto power, and it was found ; that the agriculturists were becoming tired of; repeated promises and no performances, the Government, which will, ere long, ask the eon- stituencim foes renewal of confidences and authority to further control the nation's affairs, announced with a flourish of trumpets a scheme for removing all the evils affecting their political friends in the counties. This scheme they called "The Agricultural Holdings Act," in respect of which the remarks of Mr. Rigby; our farming friends would do well to "rend, mark, learn, and inwardly digest." He said

"The Agricultuml If oldings Act is a good thing on paper, and as an essay on the mode of settlement between tenants and landlords at the termination of tenancies, but if was a t mat regret to me that the best landlords did not give the weight of their example to its general adoption by allow- ing its application to their estates. They would act upon ill principles to a man incest of dinpute, I quite believe, but great distrust arises from their coldness lathe measure, and at this time of depression especially, when every encourage- ment to enterprise in farming is needed it will be disastrous if it or a similar measure is not promptly adopted. It was great blow to the hopes of tenant farmers when the Crown lands especially were contracted out of the application of the Act to sueh a large extent, and it remains inexplicable to patient lawabiding tenant farmers why they were so and why they remain so. It looked like • physician prescribing , treatment for others which lie would not under any circum- Winces adopt for himself. If the Act were made com. pulsory by law it would givegreat impetus to farming. and stimulate all possible effort just now I quite believe, or , our leading landlords would openly acknowledge the principles of the Act by its beady and general application , to their estate,"

Given freedom of cultivation, security of tenure, and compensation for unexhausted improvements, the farmers' beet way of mitigating the effects of the present depre.ion, and of meeting foreign competi- tion, is, an Mr. Rigby clearly and imprevavely re- marked, to farm better. Mr. Rigby's observations are deserving and ought to command the serious con• sideration of every intelligent farmer. He took a eomprelia.ive view of existing circumstances, .d his: facts and arguments he marshalled with telling force before the Chamber of Agriculture. His hearers hardly needed reminding of the lasses to which farmers have been latterly subjected spite the practice of the most rigid economy and self denial, nor of the present practice of landlorchf to "keep the farmer in a prescribed groove from which he cannot deviate, and count be content to take what comes" They knew full well the effects of the fetters which bind and have bound them in the past ; and simultaneous elth Mr. Rigby's condemnation of the perpetuation of these restrictions there comes the testi- mony of the well.known veteran agriculturiat, Mr. J. J. Iffechi, of the justneas of the claim for freedom of cultivation. His statement of farm accounts for the year 1879 shows a lase, as compared with his accounts of the previous year, of £7io; and this tithe first in- stance for fifteen years that he hes suffered a lons. If this veteran agriculturist, with all his experience and Imowledge, met in his farming operations last year with • loan of £7OO, it does not require a great stretch of imagination to get at the losses that many farmers less acientiflo, and more hedged about with reetrictione a 5 to cultivation, must have suffered. Mr. M•l3 is free to cultivate his farm as he pleads, and he unhemtatingly states that had he not had free dope to dispose of hay and straw as be chose, and been altogether free and unfettered, the results of his farming last year would have been worse than they were. Mr. Rigby truly remarked that r.trietiens upon

farrcing now enforced by the majority of landlords " were appropriate to the farming of a hundred years ago, perhaps, but the competitive spirit of the present age requires more liberty." These restrictions un- doubtedly breed distnvit, and where there ought to be confidence between landlord and tenant there is sus- picion. A point in Mr. Rigby's argument deserving of special demonstration was that restrictions limited enterprise, and that there could be few eases, wlmre freedom of cultivation was conceded, in which the tenant coald injure lois landlord without injuring himself— the last thing a man out of Bedlam would attempt to do.

On how to farm better Mr. Rigby offered some valuable and seasonable advice. Whilst he did not ignore the power or intportatice of foreign competition, he was by no matins alarmed about thefuture of English agriculturists. Fermero, he said, need to take more notice of IV Maher changes than ham been their wont, and to regulate their operationn in their fields bp the signs of coming changes ll° told the Chamber that in their own county of Chester, which has been famed , from time immemorial far the Excellence of Ms chaser., that " prime die.° of the best quality is made in com- paratively few of the farm lion.e of the county. It is eetimated, indeed, to be less than one-fourth of the total make; another fourth, called good Cheehire, is not bolter than the average good American and the remainder io w‘roe." This is a strong indictment against the cheese-makers of Cheshire, and Mr. Rigby appropriately pointed out to the Chamber that in any case the fanners could meet foreign competition better with the best quality of cheers than with poor or even a fair average, as people would al- ways pay a high price for the best cheese. But to produce the Ictst cheese a different 'practice than that which now obtains in its manufacture must be pursued. More knowledge is required in the dairy as well as in the field in these competent° times. Butter and cheese making is reduced to a mince. It is desirable, as Mr. Rigby said, that the constituent qualities of milk should be understood and duly appraised in the mind, the chemical changes it under. goes in the lamest of manufacture into cheese, how it is affeeted by the weather of. our changeable clituate in making, how much or how little certain claws of curd should be salted and how treated afterwards until ripe, for use and for market. And so in the field, for there chemical knowledge must be brought to bear, the quality of the soil understood, , as well us the kind of manures to apply and when for 'without such knowledge much time and money may be spent in vain, and thus caution, thoughtful. nese, and prudence are as needy too good farmer as enterprise and capital. The advice which Mr. Rigby intparted to the Chamber of Agriculture on this and .thee points effecting the well being of agriculturists Iwe cannot too highly commend.

div.head: COMINU SESSION AND THE QUEEN'S SPEECH.
div.p: THE COMINU SESSION AND THE QUEEN'S SPEECH.

On Thursday Parliament will be opened by the Queen in puma, and a period of more than ordinary political excite- ment will have commenced. It is said that the opening ceremonial will he made an occasion of great state, And of special attraction for the Londoners, who dearly love • goal allow. But to the country at large the event is also one of more than ordinary interest. It is many years since tire public mind has been BO agitated respecting the politi:al i situation, foreign and domestic, as it is at present. All 0,1 the country people are watching with an intense intere,d the movements of parties, and there is a vague boding of ancertainty, almost of apprehension, as to the future, not easily to be accounted for. It is telt that although there maybe peace in Europe, the foreign policy of the Beaconsfield ad- ministration has incurred responsibilitice that may at any time lead the country into great diffleoltirni and with re- gard to borne affairs there are many great questions, and questions of the first importance, coming to the front, and that, whether or not the. Government undertake to deal with them, will be sure to occupy the attention of Parliament during the coming session. The speech from the throne' is not likely to eat* the curiosity of the country with regard to the intentiogs of the tiovernment. English Royal speeches are rather mysterious documents that somehow or other invariably excite great expectations up lothe time of their delivery. But on reading them the

feeling experienced is invariably one of blank die- , appointment. They never rise above the merest common place, the chief aim and object of the authors being to aviod giving any indication of the Governmental policy to be pur- sued during the session that is to follow. A collection of Royal speech. would possibly have been a valuable addi- tion to the " Curiosities of Literature," by "Discaeli the elder," and as model. for teaching studenta to frame sentences to coaceal their thoughts, might be studied with ladvantage. It is by no means likely that the coining epeech will prove to be say exception to the general rule., or that !' there will be touch in it, even for those who profess to be , able to read between the lines, to indicate the intentions of the Government on any of the great questions that are now pressing fort solution. Indeed, it is most proluble that the Premier, in sketching out Her Majesty's speech, will depart from this tantalizing old custom of giving ' te the country as little information PS lie possibly can with regard to the views of the Government on the state of affairs • either at borne or abroad. Yet there are such a variety of' topics to which the early attention of Parliament will have to be directed, that some important reference to them cannot ; well be avoided. One great object in the composition oft Royal speech is to paint things as much as possible in the "coloured the rose." We may take for granted.that foreign affairs, or rather our foreign relations, will dealt with in the uaual congratulatory paragraphs. Her Majesty's faith- ful Commons will be congratulated on the fact llmt we are 1 at peace with all the groat powers, and that we have Web- lidiStl friendly relations with all the courts of Europe. It will be rather difficult to frame a sentence describing our I relations with, or prapects in Afghanistan as at all aatisfac- , • tory, but in all probability the country will be assured that a settlement in" approachiug." South Africa can be tr.ted of in a still more hopeful strain and credit will probably be taken for having brought the lulu war to a successful for. mination. If the differences with the Boers be referred to at all, it will most likely be for the purpose of making it appear that they are at an end, and that, on the whole, the prospects of South Africa are of the most hopeful demrip- hon. An assurance will probably he given that the Govena- I ment la using its best endeavours to carry out the promised reforms in Turkey ; and we may safely affirm that little or no notice will be taken of the obstacles that have presented themselves, or of the accumelating evidence that there is on every side of the hopelessnes. of Lord Beaconsfield's self- : imposed task ever being carried out. Of course, we ehell be congratulated on the signs which have appeared of a trade revival ; but `.chemicals," ere may prophesy with aefety, will not be brought forward on this ...ion as evidence of , the extensive and permanent character of the improvement. The most serious difficulty that the Government will have , to deal with during the coming session is the state of ; Ireland ..and there is no paragraph in the Royal Speech that will be scanned with greater curioeity than the one referring to this painful subject. Roomers have been rife to the effect that the introduction oft measure dealing with the land question in Ireland it contemplated by the Govern- ment, but nothing has transpired to mad to the supposition that tlae statement has been made on any reliable authority. Phe probability is that an expression of regret at the pre- vailing distr., and an assurance that amens will be found to meet it until the return of prosperous times, will be the stun and substance of the amount of consolation that Ireland will receive. The session, ucording to all appearance., promiees to be a stormy and eventful one throughout, and there are signs that frmn the outset the Home Rule party will prove more troublesome and unmanageable than ever The Opposition leaders have a long list of indictments to bring against the Governtnent, and whatever form their attacks may take, it is manifeat that, al- though in a minority, in debating power they will have a groat advauMge. Votes of censure and of want of confidence in ministers can be easily negatived by the corn. pare, Conservative majority that will support ministers to the bitter end; but the discussions will be watched by the ' country at large with a keener intereat than has been mani- fested in parliamentary proceedings during any year aloes the Conservatives have been in office, and it will be strange , indeed if the effect of them discussions will not he most damaging to a government whom blusterings and bragga- docio during the past year have been only equalled by their unhappy blundering, and disaatrous failures in well nigh every quarter of the globe.

The Cheshire Tory papers ore ill high glee. They hare made the curious discovery that the. Liberal atMck" on the representation of Mid-Cheshire has collapsed, and that no Liberal candidate will be brought forwald at the nest general election. We hare no objection to our Tory friends enjoying themeelres for the time being in this foole paradise. Their eyes will be opened quite time enotigh. Meanwhile it may be ae well tests. that we bave it on the best authority that the *Libe-ral attack' is not only pro- greesing, but that on no former occasion have Liberal pros- pects throughout the county looked brighter. Front all quarters we receive encouraging reports. It is very gener- ally admitted that there is • real majority of Liberal elector, no that the returnee at least one candidate eppose,j

div.head: TOWN TALK.
div.p: TOWN TALK.

It is not Overy long thne ago since people in the town of Whine. were in the habit of exercising their privilege, as Englishmen, to grutuble at the fact that all persems suffering Irono any serious accident had to he taken to Warrington or Liverpool hospitals. In the face of some considerable op- position, the existing Whims Accident Hospital was erected, and I venture to my that it is fitted up in a manner which will bear tke cloaest inspection. and IfiliCil does infinite credit to the promoters. It in, therefore, not to be wondered at that Mr. Well. loudly compLiined, at the last meeting of the Local Board, 0183 there seemed to be a prejudice against the institution, as he had noticed on several occasions that men who had met with serious ini,haps were sent en to Liverpool. He ruferred particularly to a case where a poor signalman, employed by the London and North-Western Railway Company. toothed 133 rt of one of his feet cut off whilst doing hia work at the Widnee station, and had been acne Oil to one of the Liverpool hospitals whet. he died. Now there are hundreds of crippkil men in the country who hare recovered from far more serious accidents than Ibis. The question very naturally arises bow iii, that men of such large experience and scientific knowledge as the medical ataff of oue of the largest hospi•als in the country should have loon baffled by such 3. simple cam, and per- mitted the poor sufferer tootle nods: their hands. Etrhape it may he nee nary to brietly refer both, report of the en. cident ot loch I read in your columns at the iiine. As the signalman no, only a servant occupying an inferior position iu the employ of the ..,:ompany, the pden employed on wine lines of immedi- ately sealing mach a patient on to the nearest hospital byan express engine, which takes precedb nee of all hot one does of trains, was not pursued. Dr. trheeffe was ant for, and consulted as to in hether the men would be able to bear removal to Liverpool. He gave it 33 his opinion that he would, 331t1 the signalman wan then carried from Ike Company's to the Central Station, and sent on by trainee Liverpool. Many persons on reading this may he inclined to blame Mr. Peters, the station master, for not having the man immediately sent to the Widnes Hospital, instead of permitting him to become weaker and weaker before he could be attended to by a surgeon But it roust not be for- . gotten that he is only a servant, responsible to a district manager awl a Board of Directors ; and he, therefore,cannot pursue a course which would be oppmed to the interests of his employe s, who are probably subscrihersto the Liverpool hospitals, :and not to the Vt'idnes one. loin highly probable that when the injured man arrived at the Liverpool institu- tion he would not here, well prepared to benefit by the trmtment, especially if he met w-ith a follower of the teamed Dr. Sangrado. as he would have lost such a quantity of blood that his systeni would be too enfeebled to battle 'Lwow- fully with his general weakness. In fact, Ido not see how, under the circumstances he could have recovered if Ile bad ever had the advice of that learned phyeician 11th. report that the London and North-Western Railway. Company are not subscribers to the Widnes Hospital he Onto. the sooner they become so Alld the tricker they be placed in a position which will enable them to obviate any such difficulty in the future. ST. HELENS AND THE DISTRESS IN IRELAND.

It is to be regretted that the rneeting held in the rown Hall on Fridsy evening for raising funds for the relief of our distressed brethren in Ireland was not more largely at- tended ; but there can be no doubt that through the medium of the press the sympathies of the people of the town will be reached by the decision of the meeting that prompt aid is necessary for the starving population of the Sister Isle. 1 he picture given at the meeting ho Mr. W. simpson, of Liver- pool of t .e harrowing scenes of desolation and suffering he had been witness of cannot fail to move even the I most callous to an act of generosity on be- half of the poor people whose hardships Mr. Simpson detailed. A {.hasing feature in the meeting was to hod representatives of all sects and creeds harmoniously joining in sympathy with the poverty-stricken people of Ireland and recognising in them a common brotherbooe. The tnorement which has been set on foot, we doubt not, will be in-oduetive of an amount of practic d sympathy with Otto distressed th.tt will do credit to St. Helen,; and our

hope is that that sympathy. as well as the generosity of the , people of other towns in England, may reach the shores of Ireland in time to stay the pangs of hunger and arrest the ravaget of distase which 31r. Simpson to touchingly described. Collections are to be or have been made in most of the works of the town, and other means hate been adopted foe obtaining the donations of the charitable.

Seniors CRAINIC AGAINST A RUNCORN BERRNIMIRR.— Joseph Pegg, of the Sloop Inn beerhouse, Lockwtreet, was summoned for knowingly permitting his premises te be the habitual resort of reputed prostitutes, they having been allowed to remain there longer than was necessary for the purpose of reasonable refreshment. —Sergeant Hantlford said that on the Iftth inst. he was on duty in Lock-street, anti he instructed P.C. Ilibbert to go into the house. From what the officer told lien when be came out, he remained in the street from moon o'dhek till twenty minutes past eight. He also went into the beerhouse, and in a rootn on the right band side found seven sailors and two prostitutes. He then left the neighbourhood, hut he had the house watched either by himself or another officer from twenty minutm past eight to ten minutes past nine. The two women seen in the place were Elizabeth Owen and one known as 'Cuckoo," both of whom had been convicted. He told the laullord that he should have to report him, upon which he said there was nothing wrong going on there—P.C. Lowndes gam evidence as to visiting the defendant's holm at 20 minutes past eight and after nine o'clock, on the night of the 190 h inst., , and finding a large number of milt re and the two women in the mom.— P.C. Cooper said that 04 visiting the place with P.C. Fryer at 20 minut,w past tenon the night of the lltth het, he found one proatitute and 14 sailors in • room.— ' P.C. Fryer corroborated the evidence of l'.C. Cooper.—Mr. Lewin appeared for the defence, and argued that the police had failed to prove that the beerhouse was the habitual re- sort of prostitutes, or that the two women had remained there on ally other night an unreasonisble• time for refreshments. —The defendant was called, and mid that on the 1916 net, the young woman Owens was assisting his wile to serve the sailors, who were lodging there. it being a regular place for them to board. He had often as many as fourteen sailors 'odgsng with him. Iti. wife paid Owens la Id. for the work she did. lie had never had any . complaints made to him about permitting women of ill fame to frequent his premises—Mra. Pegg told that Elisabeth Owens was engaged by her (witness's) daughter to assist on the 19th inst , owing to her illness—Elizabeth Owens stated on the 19th inst. she acted as charwoman for the defendant, and received le. Id. for the work.—Wm. Kidd, sailor, mid he now Miss Pegg engage Miss Owens to help at chating, and she remained there to mangle. He noticed Emma Boatock there, but she diet not remain more than a quarter of an hoist—The magistrates then retired, and net their return into court, the chairman said the Bench had given the case the most mreful couslderation, as they felt it was one of the greatrel importance in many rearwcte, the defendant being charged with an offence which was liable ten very heavy penalty, and to have to submit to the emiorsing of his license. 'Plie case was certainly one of extreme suspicion, anb the police had acted perfectly right in taking the action they had. The magistrates, however, did net consider the evidence of each A nature as to allow them to come to the dec:sion that the defendant bed habitually allowed his [ite- mises Onto the resort of prostitutes.—Undor all the circum- stances, they thought it better to give the defendant the benefit of the doubt, and the summons would a“ordingly be dismissed.

div.head: VAGARIES OF A PRESCoT lIUSBAND.
div.p: THE VAGARIES OF A PRESCoT lIUSBAND.

At the Premot Sessions, on Tuesday, before Messrs. J. Bibby and W. L. Evans, James Ryland., &young man living at Present, was eummoned for not maintaining his wife, who is chargeable to the Prescot Union, and who requires relief. —Mr. Swift &lid that in this cast he appeared on behalf of the limardiens of the Prescot Union. The defendant wee summoned under a recent All of Parliatnent, which was 30 for as material in those word. When • married woman requires relief without her husband the linardians of the Union to which she becomes chargeable may apply to the Metice, and thereupon such justice's may !amnion such husband to appear before them to show cause why an order should not be made to maint.tin his wife ; and upon his ap- pearance such justices may, on hearing such wife upon oath, or receiving sue . other evidence as they nor deem sufficient, make an order upon him to pay ench sum weekly, or otherwise, towards the cost of the relief of the wife." In this case the parties had been married about 18 months, and had one child ; and for the first five month. after they were married they lived with the father of the husband at Whist., but after that time they took a house for themselves in Present The hustund, however, became very idle and dissolute, and upon one reckoning Saturday he did not go home with las wages, and his wife went in search hf him and found him in a public-houm drunk, and his arms round the waist of a womau well known in the town as a loose character. She spoke to him, but he threatened her. She went away out he followed her, and told her that ehe need not go home for if she did he would turn her out. She went home to her father's, and her brother and cousin pro- o ericd to the house of the defendant Rylande, and knocked j at the door. Rylands shouted out that she need not come there, he evidently thinking that the person at the door was • his wife. The brother and cousin, however, went in and Bylaw's came down stairs in his shirt. The brother (Joseph Berry) slaked him wlkat woman he had got in bed, to which question Ryland, plied that he had got no woman in bed at all, and if he liked to see he could go and look. They went together into the bedroom Ryland& leading with a ' candle in tale hand. Having got into the room Ryland.' said "Now, look, are you satisfied?" Witness said it,, was , not satisfied yet, and he looked under the bed and there found a woman undreesed. He afterwards went to his wife, admitted hie wrong, cried over it, and persuaded hie wile to go hack to him. She went for a little while, hut on account of hie conduct she was obliged to go home again and from that time to this he had been tbe regular associate of com- mon women. As the law formerly stood there was no Act , of Parliament to punish • hueband for deserting hie wife except the Vagrancy Act, and there was no Act of Panic.' went to enable their worships to make an order. But the present 001 w,, passed to supply the deficiencies which pre- , viously exieted. Rubin& could formerly in AOOlO name' defeat the Vagrancy Act by going into court and saying eel that defendant says " torn quite willing to keep her," no matter what he had done. But under this Act of Pattie- , ment that idea was not available or of any weight whatever. Very soon after that Act was pawed there was the caw of Thomas againet Allsop, end it was decided that an order be made for the maintenance of the wife (who had left her' hustund on :iceman: of illusage) notwithstanding that he' promised te take her back.—Jeines l'arkinson, relieving officer for the Premot Union, then proved that the Guar- dians had granted Ins• • week to defendant's wife. Ellen Rvlands, wife of the defendant, quite a young woman, ami Joseph Berry and William Berry were then called, and fully corroborated Mr. Swift's etatement.— Maggie Renshaw gave similar evidence. The Magistrates made on order of 10s. per week.—On hearing the &Melon, the defendant muttered that he could not pay it it wu an impossibility.

The colon were very well rendered, and ! • embrae.l such songs as the pathetic °Little sister's gone to sleep" the effect of which was wonderfully enhanced by a choir of girls singing the chorus in a subdued tone), and "'I he little maid and her bonnet," snug by a boy w ith great effect, and described the vicissitudvs of a new bonnet, to hich no completely turned the little wearer's head that wlivn she arrived late at church the choir were singing ° Hallelujah!' and, thinking everybody knew of her new bonnet, thought they were singing, °Hardly knew. you," and then left on the best of terms with herself. The bond gave several selection., which gained great applause. The choir-master, Mr. R. H. Mille, wed as conduemr, and Mr. Stephenson anon most efficient accompanist, besides supplying the bass in the con-1 celled pieces with taste and power. During the evening the I boys went through a memory lesson on the systeno employed by the renowned Mn. Stokes, whicb showed great skill on the part of the pupils. At intervals Mr. Stephen.en gave short addresees on the work of the Home and its claims on the benevolent. He said that when he went to London no, minister first he was confronted with many strange sights and sounds; Pad the des:Ration around hint led hint to to something towards helping the p.,cor children, and he hired a sonall house and began that work with two outcast children. The cam* fuel grown, and during the ten years he had been engaged in that work 1,000 children kid been received. 500 of whom were then earning their own living, and 500 re- main in the Hoine or in one of its branches under training. and instruction. There were three principles mmn which the work was carried out. First, religion. Second, the family life wan regarded as the foundation of proper train- ing. As Dr. Guthrie load mid to kite, °God never intended children to be brought up in flocks, but in families." Hence their Home wee vastly diffcrent to most institutions, which worn half barrack and half workhouse: and he woe con- vinced that their scheme of having the children grouped in families was superior to the seitn-inilitary management. Third, the children were trained to industries—to tannin, carpentry, and other pursuits. He add that, as his reason for awealing to the whole country for help, they received children from all putts of the land, and said theta Runcorn friend had brought the ease of an orphan in the town before his norico, who would he intralticed into the Mine in the one se of a fortnight. He concluded by expressing his thanks to those ladies and gentlemen who had contributed PO largely towards making that entertainment so great a !succ,n, and especially to those friends who had furnished hmnes for the boys and girls during (heir stay in Runcorn I and Widnes. Alderman Davers moved the following resolution with reference to the Liverpool Vl'eterworks Bill. 1880 That this Chamber expresses its satisfaction in hearing that the Corporation of Warrington will take the necessary steps to obtain clauses in the Liverpool Corporation Waterrrorts Bill, , IPSO, requiring that the water pipes croffiing the Mersey I near Fiddler'. Ferry shall be sunk too depth sufficient to prevent any obstruction to the Dreamt or any proposed im- provement in the navigation of the river." In moving the resolution he said the Warrington Town Council bad thought it neerssay, in the interest of the borough, to lodge a formal petition against the Liver- pool Corporation Waterworks Bill. By that bill it was pre- I posed, in bringing the water to Liverpool, to crow the Mer- eey with the pipes about a mile below Fiddler's Ferry, and to deposit them in the mud. To guard against the possibi- lity of their interfering with the future improvement of the navigation of the river, it was proposed to ask for the Meer- tion of clauses in the bill requiring the Corporation to place the pipes Cl such a depth as would not interfere with the improvement of the river. This was the kind of subject which it was proper for the Chamber to take up ; and, the Corporation having already moved in it, it would be satisfactory to them to know that thc Chamber of Commerce approved of their action. /le.ar. hear.) As to the obj. the Aseamiation they would no doubt want emus tittle planation. It was for the promotion et literature, win, awl art. LPerature true really, in plain Saxon, an !MIMI, lation of all the knowledge of all the ages from the begin- ning of time. It was a record of everything that had been done bv nations and peoplee aml of men, and of the expari- ence of the poet. Hy it we came in conmet with nten of imagination and made acquaintance with every great man and every patriot who had adorned the history of the pest (Hear, hear.) By the experience of these great and noble • men we should be able to guide our lives and farm our , characters and the result would amply repay us for the labuur andtoil of research. There SW another thing which was, invaluaLlete a man whomredabout historyandrmearch. He could go to every country and every people that existed at the present day, awl study their manners and habit.; revel in the most heatitiful scenery, and have hie mind stored with a! great variety of knowledge. It surely was not too numb to compare a men of that stemp with • lazy good.for-nothlng, who cared for nothing but to eat, drink, and for ninth. There wee as much difference between them 5 there was between the galleries of the Vatimn—which he imposed were the most megniticent galleries known in the world— and a nasty Turkielt hovel ; awl the advantages which a man of literature, who ardently and pereistently pursued Ids work, had over one who entirely and thoroughlr neglected literature was incalculable. He asked thenc present whether the life of nations had out been influenced hy those who bed Medi.' literature, science, and are, In the Elimbethian age, which was a time when literature, science, End art took a new lease of tin., they would remember that those great men who then flourished were educated and accomplished, and aome of the greatest deeds of English history and some of the greatest discoveries could be traced back to them. (Hoar, hear.) Ile woold for a moment draw their attention to science. Of course there were several gentlemen who woold follow him, and he hoped thew would take up that qneetion in nylon, scientifle meatier than he might do. At the same time, he thought something about ecience would be expected from him as president of the Aesociation. Science seemed to him to be aetuelly the working of the laws of nature—a perfect knowledge of the laws of nature. Science 'teethe ticaffelding, he might wty, on which every nation bad been built up: it had contributed to the pros- perity and constitution of nations meet tlf merge he daredaay many people would say "It, there w ts no Beiellee before the nineteenth Century ; the Toone men of the nineteenth century understand geolou, ch'emistry, and what not. It wanner doubt an enlightened age, bat as • matter of fact, real science existed probably for thouaende of yearn before the present day. (Hear, hear.) The magician, of Egypt were probable grmt in science, end the (llialdaemer, also in their time. Ile supposed that Greece was consider- ably litererv, certainly scientifle. Some people said that the whole of tICe present stt ucture of society reseed on the Roman empire, but it neented to hint that the Roma,,, had imitated them who had gone before, and as far as castor., =mere architecture, aft, and even their weapons and arms were con- cerned, they had imitated the Grecians. For years science and art stood still, because the Romans cared for rear; they studied the art of IT., and developed the art of governing nations. War was the greatest enemy against literature. By war the tre,turee of knowlidge and beauty lied been sacrificed; palaces, templee, and libraries had bees burnt, awl • those eivilisetions of the 'allele great, as we possessed ill England, had been lost, nothing being left but broken pieces of pottery, or some old tower. It was quite clear tied the greateet foe to science and art was war, and they were hoetile to each other. Science tended to make nations. one family, and it was easily to be seen that the present achievements of science aunt art were uniting together in a tinst wonderful way all the people of the earth. Take, for instence, the rail- ways. We were accustoms' to ride on the railway, ansl saw the railway carriege as it passed our windows. With the railways came the telegraph, and with the newspapers, the peony poet, and these four. influencen were wonderful in binding together the world.. The Englishmen of fifty years llgOlValll taught to look upon the Frenchman as the very devil incarnate but there was not very much difference between us.
