manuladoriee for twoor three ymrs before essaying to under- take the superintondenceof an ordinary dairy. In any case we , can rneet foreign competition better with the beet quality of cheese than with poor or even with a fate average. Our people will per a high price for the best cheese when trade ' is good, and we should, therefore, try to make all our cheem I into the best. We have the great advantage of being on the .put. Milk i.e delicate article minty damaged by rough handling, by unclean vessels, and by foul smells, and we can more easily avoid them than can many of our competitors. In the matter of butter making we have even more to do than in cheese, if we would keep pace with improvements which are being male M its manufacture abroad. The dif- ferenees in results obtained in two competitive trials I have had to deal with were very great. Half a pound more butter was got out of 21 paunds of milk of miter n quality in one churn than in another at the final trial between seven of the best clmrns at the Bristol show of the Royal Agricul- tural Society, and one pound more out of 20 pounds of cream of uniform quality than was obtaMed front another , churn which gave the emallest yield oat of 15 that were tried under the same conditions ; and the quality of the butter so trade varied as numb as 231. per pound between the best and the worst. The quantity of butter from 40 gallons of whole milk, Cr.lVOli or soured, as is door in Cheshire or Lancashire before churning, was in one case 8 the. 7 om.; in another, $ Its. 9 on.; and the quality varied nearly as much min the other cam. Twenty dozen quarts of milk, treated on the Swartz system at our Manchester show last year, set in deep pans which stood in water cooled by ice for 24 hours, yielded, on three mccessive days, 10 lbs. 10 lbs. 12 In, e and 12 the, of better. The same quantity of milk, treated on the English system, cot in shallow pans for 24 hours, yielded, respectively, 12 be., 10 the. 2 ozs.. and 10 lbs. $ one. I mention these facts to show how much more thought and knowledge requires to be applied to the subject than is usually given, and to lead to the inference t theta mote perfect knowledge of the principles on which this and other works reel would, if acted upon, help to miti- gate our tomes, and to enable an to compete more success- fully with our opponents. In the matter of cultivation and management instanced, feat only urge a similar reflec- tion. Rigid economy in outlay and expenses must be practised to enable us to hold our own in the r.tce bet not that hired known as "penny wpm and pound Imaish." The land should be kept fairly dem at any cost. Thorough- ness mat still be the rule in cultivation, and liberality in the trettment of stoek and in the application of manure : but here again knowledge is required, and judgment must rule. We hare all heard the tale of the young farmer going to an hid one and asking the qusetion, " When it would be the best to put lane manure on his land ;" and after sundry trmtings to hoer, receiving for answer, "Always and coy time." But there is a time which is better than any time, and a manure that is better for a given purposee than other Linde ram:inure are. There are seasons when we may hope to get a goal return for a plentiful supply of manure, and memos when it is sitnply throwing money away to spend it, particularly in come kinds of artificial manure. To put nitrate of soda, an eam eolvent, on light lands in wet masons is to ensure it being washed through the soil quickly into the drains ; and to put volatile manures, like Peruvian gum, upon land in a dry time is to get little return, bemuse ttf the speedy evaporation of its ammonia; and it is possible to expend largely in these and other mtiticial manures, noel not farm profitably. Caution, thoughtfulness, and prudence are as much a nermsity to a good farmer as enterprise and out- lay. May I add the expresaion of my conviction, that as Limo goes on farmers ;nest cultivate brmder views of their occupations, and be more quick to 311:11.( themselvm to meet the altering requirements of the public. Some lauds in the country, as; previounly remarked, are well adapted to the growth of fruit anal v,getaules. Why .11011111 DO{ the county grow more of the bro.' i, rhubarb, asparagus, spring cabbages, green peas, and even the watercreeses that tied melt ready sale in Manchester and Liverpool? Mr. Page, in his prize essay on the fruit and vegetable snarly of Manchester. says that tons of water cress. are sold daily in tlmt town. Of as,mragns, 100 hampere have been sold in a morning by one salmtnan alone, and 1.500 sacks of gmen peas per day. Of new potatoes, as wo know, vast quantitiesare mld, many of which are grower within DO miles of them towns. There were 22.250 hampers sold iu Manchester i• one week last year, and be- sides those sent from Cornwall, Jemmy Yorkehire, Ayrshire, Per.h, Lancashire, and Cheshire, there came misty five million ems. from Hamburg and nearly eight million cwle. from Urertmny, France, Itelgiunt, it. It is well to try to realise them figures, and to understand the demand there is for tide Isinel of produce. aluch of it is not dirlicult to cul- tivate, and ought to yiell more remunerative returns than it can de to the grower cuter distant. Shall I aim add that all this proves tlmt to take full advantage of our position in the futur we must plumte our mns more highly, and try to make them good Imaistess men, lir well as farmers of the land. Sharpness and quickness often explain the difference between a successful 1111,1 an unsuccemful fanner, and there is nothing like education for stimulating and guiding the growth of the faculties. Very quietly, though very surely, is the education of all clasaes going tri, and I rejoice in the fact ;but, while the son of the labourer is receiving a better education than formerly, that of the farmer's son must be progremive also. It has been ocmsim of much regret to the Council of the Chamber that the scheme of education originated by them at Sandbach curl not secure larger attendance of scholars than twenty in me year front among this class; but, as the necessity of education in realised, apathy will, I hope, give place to earnestnese ; and I trust the day is not far distant when it will be the ambition of the farmer to give his son all the advantagm of education which lee cm obtain, as he will surely need them in the competitive race of the future. I have not touched upon the management of etock either for the dairy or for the butcher, or upon the other topics of farm managetnent which might be usefully dimussed in their bearings upon the question ; and perhaps it would hare been sufficient, and none the less useful by mason of its brevity, to !rave answered the question categorically, and said, "Tier beet way of mitigating the effects of the present depression and of meeting foreign competition is to farm better." Taken in its comprehensive sense, this is all that can be mid ; but in drawing thin conclusion it is just pos. eible—indeed, very prolethle—that very many will ask, " Hew can mu) We should. like to um more manure, grow hmvier and more valuable crops, but we have not got the money wherewith to purchase, ' mad in many mses it would be absolutely true. I name it to bespeak the considerate aid of landlonle to mach cases. Many landlonla have done libe- rally in the return of 10 and 20 per cent. of the lmt half year's rent'. but this, while a grateful and appreciable help to every tenant, and one that will necessitate retrenchment and self-denial to many landlords, probably is a small pro- portion of the losses of most tenant,. It can only have been in very exceptional cases that the rent was cleared from the farm last year, and it would be no exaggeration to say that I. the team the lore on the year's transactions would be more than the rent. I doubt, indeed, if any of us have yet fully retained the extent of our losses in their premnt and future hearings. Permit nee to say, also, that tenants may be aasiated by their landlords in their future action by re- laxing or removing all the reetrictions upon their farm- ing which may fetter then; in ever so small a degree in its profitable nimagement. Macy of our landlords impose no restrictions whatever upon the cultivators of their and or the sale of its prolum, but many do, and some of them area real hindrance to the energy and enterprise of their tenante. The sale of hay and straw is still absolutely for- biddeo on some estater. An address was delivered on Monday evening last by Mr (LW. Latlmin, of Bradwall Well, at the T wn Hall, Nan, wich, on "The Coming Election." The chair was occupied by Mr. Henry Martin, and there was a large attendance. Mr. LATIUM commenced by saying that Nantwich had . b -en always true to the Liberal cause, and he was confident that the good old town would to right when the thy of trial calm. He came there that night and chose for the subject of his lecture, "The Coming Election," because he believed that on that election, and what it would bring forth, de- pended the future of England. The most tremendous issues were offered in them that had been offered ' since the BA of the Atnerican war. On that election would depend whether England was to continue great, whether she was to have an influence amongst the nations of the world or not; whether honesty was still to be the characteristic of English statesinen. And so lie came to talk to them about the coming election, and the issues un which it must, in his opinion, turn. The first question they would ask him wee, When would this election come? He confessed he could give no answer to it. He believed that Lord Beaconsfield himself did not know. He witt a gentleman the other &IV, a candidate fore northern borough, and asked him when the election was to be, and his answer was, that he had net two gentlemen that morn- ing, both likely to be . well informed, and one told him it would come off in April, and the other in February, 1881. (Laughter.) But there were some thinr,s which might delay the contest. In the first place it was possible enough tliat if they went on agitating the country in the various towns and boroughs, and if intending canditates came down to make speeches amongst the constituents, the gentlemen who had to attend to their Parliamentary duties—very likely Conservative members of Parliament—would go to the Whips and say, We cannot stand this; there is a constant expense and letting out of money, and we most have an election." It was possible that pressure would he put upon Lord Beacona- field to dissolve ParlMment, bemum the agitation in the country was so intense. Of course, Lord Beaconsfield might wait for better Bates, better trade, for a titne when his Government could get out of the various muddles In which they now are; but bearon knew as soon as they got out of one muddle they mit into another. They might think it poseible and right to delay until there had been something settled in Afghanietan, or some signs of Eastern matters to be finishes'. (Hear, hear.) to the next place he would ask on what issues was the cooing election to be fought? The first issne on winch it must bo fought was our foreign police, for the reason that the Government made it an excuse for doing anything cod doing nothing. If they taxed Lord Beaconsfield's Govern- , meet OF any of its members with running up a tremendous !lot, bill and not paying their debts they replied, - Look at oar splendid foreign polity" (Laughter.) If fold they did nothing with domestic reforms they turned round aud said, "lion can you expect it when we- have got your foreign policy to look after?" (Laughter.) They might remember that in Sir Walter Scott's `Bride of Lammer- moor. " an old retainer, Caleb Relderstone, lit an imaginary tire and pretended to burn down the Castle of Ravenswood in order to make an excuse for the poverty of the house. If anybody asked, "Whet has become of the hunily plate? " he was referred to the great fire of Ravens- wood. If the roof was off the house the same plea was urged. And so it was with the foreign policy of the present tiovertiment—it was the eternal excuse for doing anything and doing nothing. Like Old Caleb Balderston° they were content with one excuse—he not only gut up a Me, but when there wm no wine in the house he tumbled down as if he had spilled the wine, and made (fun excuse that there was nothing to let before the guests. (Laughter.) The Government, if asked why they did not oarry various Acts through Parliament, laid the blame on the obstruction of the Irish nientbers. But he would pass front the foreign policy of the Government to 0 hat must ho. another special issue at the forthcoming election, namely its fioance. He knew that figures were wmrisome things for a public meeting, And therefore he was not going into them that night ; but of this fact they were certaim that at the present moment the Conservative Government were spending eight millions a year more than Mr. Gladstone's Govern- luent ; they had incrmsed the floating debt front five conic millions to 24 millions, and there was an undefined bill of some millions coining in for what wee going on in Afghan- _ . . . by our „is 801130 ineremed
in. And all .'this had been causes] by our interference with foreign countries. Perhaps some ' - -.•-•

two or two and a half millions of ~ . charge had been caused by the extra cost of education and subsidies to local rating,but the rest had entirely gone to military and naval preparatione in order to lkoM up our interference with foreign powers. He would read an extract from a speech which be thought put this thug in a very cleat-light, and the authority of which he did not suppose their Jingo friends would dispute:— •• This policy," the speaker said, "uf perpetualty m,ddling in every part of the world, causes disturbance, and cluße- quently leads to increased estimates. Into told that this is a very spirited policy, that there is nothing like making the influence of Englaud felt, and there is nothing of which an Englishman should hero proud a. to find he is thoul Roman cilisen in any part of the world. flow can you look forword to getting rid of the income too, unless you exerciae strict control over the conduct of the Government with respect to interference with foreign countries?" That speech was made by Mr. Disraeli in Buckingliamehire in 1857. (Ap- plau..) A Daniel come to judgment! They would re- member in the Merchant of Venice the delight of the old Jew when he found that the Paige was on his eide, because he thought that out of his own mouth he would be condemned. And so with Lord Beaconslied. He declared that interference in foreign politics must lead to embarrassed finance, owl lid it Was impossible to keep up so-celled English prestige without a warlike policy involving increased estimates. (Applause.) So far, then for the two grand cardinal points of the Liberal Creed— , peace and retrenchment. And now for the third point which they held to be necessary, that of refortn. (Cheers.) What retort. could they hope to get from a Liberal Go- vernment ? They had seen that the present Government had been in power for nearly six purr, and yet during that time nut a single domestic reform of any consequence had been elaborated by it. Bill after hill had been brought in and shunted, and we were no better off, except in the minutest particulars, than we were before the present Go- vernment came moo power. Mr. Cruse had passed a bill for iinproving artisans dwellings, and there was also the Agri. cultural Holdings Act, and others of that sort which had proved the veriest shame ever put upon the statute book. He would not refer to the reforms which he wished to see car- ried out, and that ouly a Liberal Government could carry out ; hut he Would take those which the leadms of the Liberal party hail announced themselves ready to accept at once, and which therefore they might fully expect to see carried out aeon as they came into power. And the tirst of throe reforms was the equalimtion of the county and borough franchise. It was absurd to attempt to go into a logical argument upon this subject. The whole thing was to per- fectly clear that it would bra waste of time to defend the justice or the equalisation of the franchise. How absurd it was, for instance, that the artificer of Crewe who earned as high wages as the artificer of Warrington, and was only eeparsted from him by a few miles of railway, should be without the franchise! How absurd it was that they who lived M Nantwich, and lived in better bowers for the same rent than the artisans of Manchester, should be denied the franchise, whilst the others enjoyed it because they hap- pened to live within the boundariea of a borough! There were at least 20 boroughs in England which included agri- cultural labourers and peasants amongst their constituents He was very much struck with a speech of Mr. Caine at St. Helens the other day, in which he pointed out that when he stood for Liverpool in 1874 and was defeated he polled over is,ooo votes ; but at the present time there wan an man in Parliament, except the two men who beat him, who was Teturited by as many as IB,COO votes, whereas there were seventy members of Parliament who did not poll 18,000 votes amongst thein ; cutely this was an anomaly which called for some redistribution of want, so that oopnlation might be represented more fairly than at preeent. There was alnu another reform ot which he wished to speak, and that ars the reform of the land laws. Did they think they were likely to get an honest, thorough reform of the land laws more from a Conservative than from a Liberal Government? Archdeacon Paley, a very clear-headal old not, laid down two urdinal principles about land. He mid " the first thing necessary woe to give the occupier all the power over the soil, that it was necessary for its perfect cultivation; and secondly to assign the whole profit of every improvement to the permons by whose activity it was carried on." If, thought three two principles embraced pretty nearly the entire changes which laud reformers wished to see in regard to the land laws. But take the first proposition, to give the occupier all the power over the soil consistent with its proper cultivation. flow far could that be the cahe as long as the present game laws endued? Could it be said that • nmn had power for the perfect cultivation of the soil when his produce was liable to be eaten up by vermin which he was not allowed to kill ? Then, again, had he power over the soil consistent with perfect cultivation when by a series of foolish covenants hew. obliged practically to enter itfio, otherwise he would not get the farm, he was precluded from farming in accordance with the science of modern agricul- ture ? Then, coming to fhe second proposition—maim ing Oh. whole profit of every improvement to the person by whom that activity is carried on—how could that be when by a legal 'mann whatever was put upon the soil clung to the soil ? A tenant fanner was liable to have to leave his farm when he had spent not only his hard-earned money in improving the hi manuring it and in potting u, build- ings which he could not possibly remove. True it was that tlto present Governmet t passed the Agricultural Holdings Act to remedy th..t evil but in epite of the rensonstranees and the vote, the Liberal party, a clause was put in wlichrnidtl every landlord could, if he liked, contract himself out A large number of landlord,' had availed themeelver of thin power. Even her Majesty's Government, in the ei prof. the COMrninaiOnera of Woode and Forests, the Ecclesiastical Commissioner', of whom lord Beacons- field was -one, had done to. The first necessary improvement in relation to the land laws would be the abolition of the law of distress. 'there must also be some alteration in the law of entail settlement. It had been annonnced that Her, hlajesty's Government in the next session of Parliament intended to bring too bill to make large alterations in this matter. He should like to see that bill rem much, and he wondered whether it would hoe-co permiisive clause somewhere about it. (Laughter.) Well, there were three or four questions which they ehould have to consider at the next election, such, for instance, as the BuriaLs Bill and the Licensing question. He then took a retroxpective glance at the Par- liament elected under the auspices of Mr. Gladstone in 1868, when he was Prime Minister and John Bright held office. Now this truly migh• be called the golden are of Liberalism applause)—for there never was a Parliament that did to much, wOrlred so hard, and carried euch gigantic measures. The Irish Church was disestablielied, the Irish land laws having been made more equitable the Education I Bill was pulsed, to that education was brought to every dmv—(loud applause)—purchaae in the army was abolished, ' the Endowed Schools Act was gassed, the religioue tut in! universities was aboliabed, voting was made easy and safe: IT the laming of the Ballot Act. and foreign affairs in Belgium during the Franco-German war. in Russia, the United Starr, Be., were carried on with decency ant mode, athm. Their revel., bad, :is Mr. Gladstone mid, advanced by leap 6 cad bounlo;00400 the end Ma. lilailetone woe able

anncunce a surplus of five millions. (Loud applatoe.) As a eonteast t, tans juncture Mr. Latham preseute I the present Parli tment, he asked when sort of a Parliament had they got now? He believed that it srouldgodown to history as the rudest, most disorderly, and most unmanageable Par- liamcrit that ever existed, lie then quoted from the Finan- cial Reform Almanac in onler to show that the Liberal party hoe been making steady progress. The Liberal party, he said, would have a majority of between fifty and aixty at the next general election. The electors should in Cheshire form thenmelves into as perfect an organization as possible, for if they could show a majority in this divitsien of the county or in Mid-Cheshire, it wculd Le no hard matter to secure candidates. He did not say there were not Liberals gallant and ready enough to lead the forlorn hope, and alto to light the battle, alt.mugb it was a doubtful one, Vol it was necessary for West Cheddre after 40 years of polilieol inactivity that it should have • political education through an eketion. And the better the issue,' they showed the better and more ready the candidates would Into accept the pottier. This time they couhl light under the secrecy of the ballot. When he contested Mid-Cheshire against poor Colonel Leigh, this gentleman went from meeting to nv,eting telling t:,e farmers that he would tied out how everybody voted, and the farmers believed him. When pressed as to how he could do this Colonel Leigh replied—" Because lie was sure they would tell him.' (Laughter.) The present Government was Conservative only in its jobbery. Ile believed that Cl the coining election Conservatives and Liberate alike would bite in one effort to cut done this tree which bore no fruit, and which simply overshadowed and poi.ned the ground on which it grew. They would cur in the words of an old hook, "Cut it down, why cumbereth tithe ground?" He believed , in the truth of the prophecy that the tirst day of the coring election would be Octant of the Conservative administration. (Prolonged applause.)

div.head: GU NT FROM STRETFORI?.
div.p: A GU NT FROM STRETFORI?.

Sir,—About three or four years ago Stretford was afflict , by. outbreak of contagious diseases which greatly alarmed , the inkabitante, end even disturbed the equanimity of our Leoal Board, who insittuted au enquiry. met who, i 9 casting about for a cause of the nutbreok, did, at the instigamn. pre- sumably, of their medical officer, cotne to the conclusion that one of the moat potent cause, if not the very centre if OM which the contagion radiated. was the old-established stenclaxaturated pig-killing establishment situated near the homes of the most poverty-stricken inhabitants of the village. In consequence of this wisely-directed conclusion. the slaughter house was abolished, to the intense relief of ,very inhabitant except the pig-killer, and the village ha been all hot free from fever ever since. What is alau of some consequence, we have been freed horn those ear-piere- ing squeals of concentrated agony, and the frrquent exhi- bitions of brutality, that were inexpressibly painful to every- °. whose sensibility was onto' tile most •hduratecharacter. Believing, I suppose, that public fooling was lulled into • elate of quiescence by a short immunity from annoyance and danger. • neighbouring pig butcher has lately conceived the idea—certainly highly advantageous from :his point of view—of having a slaughter house in his own back yard, wbieh is not niany hundred yards from the site of the abol- jelled establishment. This gentleman's application to the Local B.rd for the privilege of resuscitating a departed nuiaanee has been protested against both by deputation and requ-sition. Yet—l have good authority for saying it—the committee appointed by tlw Stretford Local Board has re- solved to grant the privilege, subject to the decision a the Board. If thus the Board decide. we shall be driven back to , the pestiferous condition of tenor three years ago, and the , whole of the in 'pert," in the iinmaliate neighbourhood will bu depreciated in value linen act that can only result in benefiting one inan and injuring seoren. lf, in sillne of all protests, this iojustiee should be perpe- trated, the conaequential remorse will lie heave on the conscience of our Local Board.—Yours respectfully, Blencathara, Stretford. WARD HEYS.

It may be remarked that this highly-effective picture of Lord Bescon,field proceeding to the German capital "in the midst of winter snow. and frosts and cold," to bring back twice mith honour, loses something from the circumstance that the journey was per- formed in OS middle of a pahicularly warm summer, and that at his hotel in Berlin, Lord Beaconsfield specially se- cured two beds in order that he might change from one to another during the intensely Lot nights whic lute then txUrit'ltdinisany coat lk'lir.very busy during Wednesthq not only in addreming meetings of workmen, but also in laying his views before a day's meeting of merchants, brokere, de., at the Law As.eiation Room, and to the Catholic party at the I,eagueliall. 'rae Hoses Rct.s Von—The best news in connection with the candirlature of Lord Ramsay was teublished on Wednesday. The mieunderetanding, such as it was, with headers of the Home Rule inovement, has been removed, and the whole Irish party is now as unanimous and as fervent in supporting his lordship as any other section of Liberals. The good unelenetanding was brought ahout by a little en. donation of what was intended on the one side and what was sought for on the other. It will he remembered that in his speech in Ilone Hall, and again in hie address to the electors, Lord Ramsey mid he was in favour ot extending the largest posaible measure of selt-government to Ireland enueistent with the integrity of the United Kingdom,and that he would gladly support any inquiry as to how and in what manner this could he done. 'The Hoene Rule Into not unnaturally attached great importance to this declaration. coupled as it one with the expression of a synipathy no spontaneous and lso generous that no Irishman. whether he be Home Ruler or not, could listen to it without feeling that it would be a mis- , fortune for Ireland if her BOOS could not support no mincere a friend as Lord Ratnney. i The Lit:eel/pa itercuqsays,—F.rtunately the misunder- tending has been dispelled. Lord It meaty said at Hope Hall that we Armlet give Ireland an much control over her Own affairs as the integrity of the empire would admit of, and that any restoration of the old Irish Parliament would be as impolitic as it would be distaeteful to the English, as well as to large body of the Irish people. But he is quite ! willing to support and to vote torn motion for inquiry into ' the nature and amount of the demand made by the Irish people for an Irish parliament, and this is no far eatietictory that the Hoene Rule leaders have etetermined to call their powerful organisation into full play in order to secure the return of the Liberal candidate. The an- nouncement to this effect was made by Mr. Councillor Con- nolly at the great Meth meeting in the League Hall last night ; and the presence ulam the platfortn of Dr. Comtnins (prmi- dent of the Liverpool Home Rob Association), Mr. Garton, and Mr. C. :Wardle showed that the declaration was oflicial. The rouging cheers which greeted the announcement proved that the Irish feeling in favour of Lord Ramsay is intense. No wonder that it should be so. In his lordship they have one of the staunchest friends they are likely to find in the whole range of English and Scotch politics. If he does not go quite so for with them as some Irish members, it is from no lack of sympathy with their grievances or appreciation of their wants.

TLIE lIIRPURIIEY 311:1111ER. No further light has been thrown upon the llarpurhey mystery. Haild, the man arrested al Plymouth, was on Tuesday brought up at the Manchester County Police- court, and remanded until Wednesday on the charge of per- jury in connection with his emigration papers. Co this charge he wished to plead guilty, but the plea was not ent led. Some interesting and irMmrtant sMtetnents have been made by the wife of the prisoner and three or four people who knew him, and the tendency is to clear liaild of nuspicton of the grave offence with which his name has been prmninentiv connected. Front them statements it appears that the Site, and hour, and manner of the prisoner's departure was no secret, and was known to several persons beforehand and it will also he seen that if the evidence in trustworthy the movements of Haild on the night of the murder and the while of file time are fully accounted for. The police have confronted the prisoner with several per- sons, in pursuance of their inquiry as to whether lie had any hand in the murder, and they have also submitted some of his letters to an expert, with the object of ascertaining whether there are any points of resemblance between them and the handwriting of what ie now known as the "decoy" letter. As to the molt of their inquiries the police main- tain a complete reserve. On Wednesday inoming, Robert Haild, alias Thomas Wait, was again brought up at the Manchester City Police Court on a charge of having obtained papers fur emigration purposes by false representations. Mr. Crofturo prosecuted, and formally asked for a further remand until Tuesday, which was ginned. Nothing was said to the more serious charge, but there is no doubt the police are vigorously fol- lowing it up.

div.p: TILE DISTRESS- IN I REL AND.

The news from various parts of Ireland continue. to is of the nuot appalling character. From all parts of the United Kingdom we hear of subseriptiona being made in support of the suffering pmr, :Ind the two iv flog claritable float of of the Duchess of Marlborough and the Dublin Mansion Hon.—continue to dispense relief. It is becoming more evident, however, that unless some vigorous steps be taken promptly by the Government to meet the wants of the people, the extent of the suffering will be extended and deepened to a still more appalling extent. A Cork coroner's jut), returned a verdict 011 Monday that a woman named Mary Hurley, who died suddenly, had succumbed from debility brought on from want. It was proved by a neighbour that she knew the deceased was actually starving, but that she was powerless to assist her, koiogiu want herself. The Lord Manor of Dublin has issued a more urgent appeal for funds towards the alleviation of the distress in Ireland than has yet been made from any official source. Hie lordship says them is scarcely any Irish county in portions of which exceptional privation does not exist, though it is most so • ere and general in the western counties and north-men t and sonth.west seaboards. The Lord Mayor fears that the public in England do not realke that except prompt and generoua awistance is given, tens of thousands of people must shortly die of starvation-, and complains that the sum contributed by I onion to the Dublin Mansion House Fund is lower at present than that forwarded either from Sydney or Melbourne. The Duchess of Marlborough has written to the Mayor of Leeds acknowledging the receipt of Lido from the Leeds Irish Distress Fund Committee. lier Gram says,—. It in imletsl, most gratifying to receive turbo mark of sympathy with digress from one of the most flourishing cities in England. The dirt rem is great and the need urgent." The Viceroy of Ireland has ranged to attend the Lord Mayor of Dublin's banquet on the 3nl February, on the ground of the objectionable character of the resolutions which were passed at a recent meeting over which the Lord Mayor mend 'it. The Viceroy states that it would not be in his power to ignore the reaolutions or to observe upon thorn whilst accepting the hospitality of the Lord Mayor. It is to be regretted, Cr we learn from a New York telegram, that Mr. Parnell continues to use eery violent language towards thow philanthropic ladies and gentlemen who are using every effort to collect I unds for the relief of the sufferers. Mr. Parnell delivered a speech to a large aasemblage at Buffalo, State of New York, on Monday,in the course of which he denounced both the Duchess of Marlborough's ReFef Fund and the:Dublin Mansion Haase Relief Organisation, because. as he asserted, no relief would be granted from those funds to sufferers who were in default with their rent. The speaker proceeded to make violent personal attacks upon the principal gentlemen connected with both relief organisationA all of whom he denounced by name. In conclumion, Mr. Parnell expressed his belief that I Ireland had a right to, separate nationality, and that, if it were imasible to gain tins, every Irishman ought to be ready to shed hie blood in his country's defence. Ile did not know I whether a peaceful settlement; might be obtainable, hut if not the landlords must go. Mr. Dillon loth:owed, awl resolutions were passed calling for the abolition of the feudal system in Ireland. "'" ' " ' • ' "

The American coil:ea:re for the lash distress now reaches 93,000 dole. In Thomaston, Kilkenny county, a man who had been missing for over two days was found on Wednesday by a neighbour, lying in his cabin inn state of starvation. The Duke of Devonahire has forwarded £2OO to the Lord Mayor in ald of the Irish distress hind. A further sum of has ;wen remitted by the Lord Mayor to the Duchess of Marlborough. Mn. Parnell has issued an appeal to the people of Canada urging prompt contributions through the National Land League, becsose, as he declares, the machinery of (rover, ment relief is no dilatory that thoomndn will probably perish before they are aided thereby. The mayor has agreed to welcome him to that city on the understanding that his mix- sion shall be exclusively directed to secure relief for the ma- , reran, front the distress in Ireland.

TILE LIVERPOOL ELECTION. The Conservative Press will not be able to repeat with any degree of truth its favourite assertion that Liverpool does not know Lord Ramsay. His lordship attended no fewer than six meetings on Monday. At midday he de- livend a capital speech to a meeting of working men held inn shipbuilding yard at the Brunswick Dock. The Liberal candidate made fun of the ridiculous position of Conserva- tive journaliats, who have just woke up to the fact that he is a lord, and who bring that shocking accusation against him with ponderotts seriousness. Lord Ramsay added that if he seas a lord, he was also a sailor, and asked whcher it was mt.re natural for a sailor or a solicitor to represent Liverpool. Lord Ramsay very rffectively expoeed the foolishness of pretending to take no interest in poliiivei and showed bow close was the relation between • right political policy and the material and social welfare of the working classes. Mr. IV. Rathbone, M.P., was present at the meeting, and warmly supported Lord Ramsay's candidature. Mrl ltdthly,ne said that young men were wanted in Parliament, for there were any number of e old fogeys" there already. A resolution ttledging the meeting to support Lord Ramsay wee carried with great enthusiasm, only one or two hands being held rep against it. Lord Itamsty also addressed crowded meetings on Monday night in William Henry-etreet and Erskine-street schools and Toxteth Ward. His lord- ship was over *Oily received by each audience. Tito voting constituency of Liverpool now numbers 63,046, allowing an increase on the register of 6,000 voters as compared with the general election of 1874. The Irish element is a very important one in Liverpool politics, and cotnprehends front IJ:/,000 to 12,000 votes. Opinion is a good deal divided as to the effect of the circular issued by the advanced section of the Home Role party requesting the Irish voters to abstain from taking part in this election until a candidate offers who is willing to answer in the affirmative the test question put by the Home Rule Confederation—rix. Will he support an inquiry into the nature and grounds of the demand made for the restoration of an Irish Parliament? Dr. Commit., president of the Liverpool Home Rule Asso- ciation, and the party who act with him, are not satisfied , with Lord Ramsay's general statement. On tire other hand, many of the leading Liberals ore not stall discouraged by the tlareatenl inaction of the Irish party, because they do not believe it will be geniral. The Home Rulersthemselves , are clinic led on the point, and a large number would vote : independently of the Herne Rule Association under any cir- cumstancee.

:The hobhnNation, in an article on the Liverpool elec- tion, warns the Home Rule party against pushing too far • the suggestion of returning Tones to Parliament by way of punishing the Liberals. "It is," rays the Dublin Home Rule organ, "a delicate matter to say what course on Aglo- Irish constituency should take supposing the Liberal re- tuained as inflexible as the Tory upon Irish questions (with a Tory Ministry in office). It does not follow, we think, at all no readily as a matter of course as some persons think that they should jump at once to note for fhe Tory to spite the Liberal."

mvs: —lt is no secret that the confidence with which • Littoral candidate is now attacking a Conservative seat Liverpool—an experiment to be repeated on a larger scale throughout Lancashire at the general election—is , founded upon the hope, or, rather, the certainty that Lord !Derby's influence wilt be employed against the Ministry. , Aristocratic power has held deep root in English society. !and even among active commercial and industrial communi- ties like the great Lancastrian boroughs the authority of Knowsley is potent. It must alao be recognisad that Lord : Derby Iranacquired a personal reputation for his mgaeity land hi, prudent counsel in matters lying outside the sphere of politics. The strength derived from his hereditary posi- tion 11114 his individual character Lord Derby is, it seems. prepared to use against tke party with which he was offi- cially connected for More than twenty years. This is no longer to remain an inference from such ambiguous acts a, Lord Derby's entertainment of Lord liartington during the political campaign of the latter in Lancashire a few menthe ago. It is to be made clear to all men, we are told, by the undisguised and thorough-going patronage of Lord It.anmv • '" •

..... The excitement of the political campaign commencedin right earnest on Tuesday night, when great meetings were held by both parties. The Liberal gathering at the Theatre Royal was one of the mom remarkable political demon- • swallow, which Liverpool has witnessed. 00 great was the crowd M the adjacent streets that it is said to hare Liken Lord Ramsay an h or to proceed from the Adelphi Hotel to the theatre. On his arrival at the latter place, he was received with etriking enthusiasm, which reached a climax tithe close of his admirable and spirited address. An announcement made by the chairman, Mr. R. D. Holt, that Lord Derby had intimated that he wished Lord }tamely success, was received with tremendous cheering. Lord Ramsay, who described himself as a decided Liberal Int no doctrinaire, said that he proposed to himself no Axed or final . condition towards which their efforts at progress should directed ; but among the measures of which he was im- mediately in favour were the extension of the franchise to the counties, the redistribution of seats, the reform of the land laws and liquor law., and the establishment in the counties of the system of representative institutions for the purposes of local government. He desired also that the state of Ireland should be taken up by the Goverment , that the Irish land laws should be reformed and that I-Aand should be placed upon the same frwring and [MVO the same political rights and power ot aelf-govern. merit as England at present possessed. lIEFIING IN WARRINGTON. In compliance with a requisition which was presented to the Mayor (Alderman l'ickmere) a short time ago asking hie Worship to call a public meeting for the purpose of raining funds for the relief of the distress in Ireland, • meet- ing was held in the Pubic HAI, on Wednesday evening. for that pnrpose. The Mayor presided ; anti there ware also present on the platform the Revs. E. C. E. Carlton, J. Yong*, R. Filcher, Fathers Pozzi nod Feeny, Alderman Charalley, Alderman Burgese, Councillor Crostield, Councillor Monks, Messrs. 8 Rigby, It. Davies, W. Sharpe, T. Flood, aud the Town Clerk (Mr. W. If. Brook There was only a moderate attendance.

he wee away from home. It woe regret' 1 that I shall not be able to attend the nietaing you have sum- moned in connection with the distress in Ireland. It seems to be very revere indeed, more no, I fear, than we realise. I hare letters from mv relations in that country, giving a de- I plorable account of the misery and the death anion that pre- voile, not only lathe country dietricts, but in the large towns. I eympathise entirely with your object in calling the meet- ing, and shall willingly help in any way that may be sug- gested." (Applause.) Sir Wilbert tireenall also had com- e municated with Mr. Hobert Davies that he intended to have collections in Walton for the Fame object. lie was getting an old man, and it wee ton cold and severe amther for him I to be out late at eight. (Applause, Alderman Burmese moved the next resolution, "That a combined appeal be made to the irmabitanM of this district g for funds, to to cent to the relief of the famine.stricken j provinces." Ile had very great pleasure, indeed, in asking his fellow-townsmen to contribute, no far to they could, to the relief of those of our fellow-citirens in another part of the kingdom, who were suffering from the distress that had I been desnrilo.,l Icy the gentlemen who had addressed the , meeting and lie was quite nure that appeal would not be made in vain. There never was anything approaching the dis- trese in Ireland that an appeal was nmde to the inhabitants , el Warrington to come to the rescue, hut they did what , fairly could h• expected of them, and he was quite sure they , i would not fail on this occasion. It was the bounden duty • of every one of them to come to the assistance of those people, whowere eufferlng front the viaitation al Providence. , It was not for us to say they had not been as provident they could be. We found that jhev were suffering severe privation, and, in fact in a gate of absolute etarvation and our duty was to come to the rescue in every way we possibly could. Ile should be very glad, indeed, to hid that a very hearty response w, given by the inhabitants of Warrington to the appeal that was made that night. Hewn, quite sure it was not necessary for him to take up the time of the meeting by urging upon every one of them, no far AS they could, to contribute on an desirable an object. What Ireland was muffering now might have been our rase, if we had been under the same conditions as those in which they were : hut if we found that our condition none better one than theirs, it would he a lasting disgrace to all of us were we, with , means to spare, tu allow them 40 starve for want of food. I (Appian., Rev. Father PCONT paid he quite concurred with the reso- InOon that an appeal should be made to the inhabitants of Warrington, and he was happy to soy that be moat cordially seconded that resolution. Tidortunately, the distress Istria now prevailed in the western Nrtiuns of Ireland was net an imaginary one. It Iran a stern reality the papers were to. wing with reports of the severe hardships. They had had, no doubt, hard Ctn. in Warrington, owing to the depreseion in trade, but they could safdy say the privation endured by them had been simply a shadow of what wean.. suffered by those whoor position they were contemplating. The people here suffered poverty and privation from want of cniployincet, but those were small because they were not all suffering on eceount of depression of trade. In Ireland they knew tlore were many people living !rum hard to mouth, who were dependent for their subeistence upon their daily toil, and they looked forward to thy time of harvest to male provision for winter and spring tinie. They knew only ' too well that the last season had been most disastrous, and ' the consequence w-as that they were left in a most deplorable ! etate 01 elarvation. There were hundreds and hundreds who ' were periehing if relief WM not immediately brought to ! then, Having referred to the distress in Ireland in 1647, • the speaker went on to sty that it was to our own interests to relieve the distreas, for the germs of disease were wafted across the St. lieorge's Channel and settled in this country. Therefore it was not only fur charity but for selbinterest to do what we could to make an account appeal in the country. A very short time ago he was at the bedside of a very good old man, who had since departed. Ile was About 80 years of age, and he (the speaker) was sympathising with him in bin distress and poverty, but he exclaimed that it woe nothing. • He Mid, " When tne famine came upon us in Ireland in 154 d I had not even a scrap of Wind, and on tht mountain side there I due up the wild roots, mil I used to feed upon them ,in order to keep body and soul together. Thiegs now are altered, and I look iiimn the mode of living in this country as a luxury compared with what "1 we endured." That would give them come idea sof what • lore, occurring at the pre.nt time. Those scenes were re- ' pealed, and there could be no doubt that many would perish ' unless help wae brought to them. Another thing to move , them to be generous was the fact that those poor m.ople ! could not relieve themselves in any manner whatever. They were dependent ulmn the searmns, hence it was no man had recourse to employment. They could not I.k around and find wealthy people : all around were in the came poeition, and they hoped the benevolence of the charitable would come to them and relieve thmu ito their diatrese. (Ap- plause.) Councillor F. MON., NI supporting the resolution, said , from what he saw in Ireland in Ind he knew something of the districts in which the famine we. now raging, and lie was quite ealiall,sl that there was need of their support. It I was not & question of what should be done, but what was to be done at the present moment was to prevent these people : dying from actual starvation. (Apple..., There was nothing there but bog, water, and rock, OINI bow people were going to tine-in a country like that in numbers such as they found them there, he confessed lie was at a loan to decide. • But the duty that clay was pressing and immediate, and therefore, he cordially and hentily supported the reaolution. • Mr. NT MOON. MACKIN said he would express the ex- treme pleaeure that he had, and lie was sure that they all had, in being prenent on such an occasion to give living t proof tel the fact that God really had mmle of one blood all the 1 nations that dwelt upon the earth—(applause)—and that 1 they intended to manifest that fact in a very tangible form. • conlially juine of in what was said by Mr. Davies about the special claims which the Irish as a people had upon us. . Those were claims connected with Ireland reaching tom for r . back a perial certainly 119 the commencement of this cen• • tam. We had received from Ireland some of the lineal mee that tiod ever created. They had been our generals, our statesmen. and philanthropists, and we bad at the present day on-cry large amouut from Dated of all that was bone sad sinew—all necessary for carrying on many of our large works (Appian., There wee no doubt that some of them might have felt somewhat severely the male- • dictions of Isom of the partiea connected with various movements in the Parliament, but those they forget entirely in the presem e of sorrow and suffering, and be therefore - should add hr strong recommendation to each and all of them however little it be that they could afford to give it heartily, and to remember above all things that the Grant Father of them all loved a cheerful giver. (Applause.) He had great pleasure in supporting the resolution. (Ap- ; P4:..")' • .. • . . •

The TOWN CLERK having read the requisition presented to his Worship, The MATOI.I said in accoaLuce with that requishion he bad called a town's rneetirtg, for he thought there was no • doubt that there w. very great distress non in Ireland, if I all w. true that they read in the papers. Ile had had one . communication from the lArd Mayor of Dublin saying it was so, and owing to that telegram he received from him, lie (the Mayor/ wrote to the clergy and minister. in Warring- ton asking them to give their help in collections in the I churches and chapel; to gain money to send over to Ire-1 land. They very kindly aided him in that, and Ike received very kltal letters from all of them. Some mould nettles. on the day named, hut they said they would do it afterwards. I There load been a very fair result on the whole—he thought that the hest method at the time of asking their fellow— townsmen to stilmerihe—and he thought he had better real to them the amounts already collected ----Sr. Peter's, LI 2s. , 3d.; Christ Church, Lat.hforol, ES Is. Dd.; Parish Church, IEIS 5 Id.; Cairo-street Chapel, £l4 2s. 7d.; St. Jamey's ' Church, it/ 12s. 61; St. Paul's Church,.£B 3s. 7d. The Co- operative Society had also sent hint £d. He had al. re- ceived £2 2e, that day from a gentleman who would rather not have hie name mentioned. He might say he (the folayor) hadalready subrecribed twice to the object, hut he . should be very glad to do ea again. (.kpplause.) There , was no doubt that the dietress was urgent from what they . heard, and when they came to think thor people were really for wind of something to mit, clothes to cover them, I and fuel to warm them, he thoughtthe heart of everyone most soften at their olistress. Whatever his politic. dr religion mightberhiettoeeoooghttn las open at the word of charity, , to do what he could to alleviate their suffering.. (Applauee) I He hoped the gentlemen that evening would come forward and state their opinions as la the destrability of their having n further collection in the town; and, of course, all politics or religion would be liqt in abeyance. (Hear, hear.) Let them all look at it from one poiut of view, and tel their • watchword toe "charity," and so do their best to relieve their fellow subj.!. in Ireland. (Applau.) Mr. Buena Dames said he did not attend there that night with the intention of making a speech—m mly out of loyalty to support the Mayor in the chair. Ile h. - not had the ep.rtuoity of reading manv of the accent). which had reached nr of the great Metre., but there could be no , question, th as e Mayor had said, that wi it was tleospread, and that it called upon onto notice extraordinary efforts at the present no:anent for its alleviation. They knew that the liovernment would do sotnething, but they were not accustomed in this country to appeal to the Government every occasion for charitable aid. They came to private sources, and they knew tloat when 1100t1 case was made out . the liberality of the British people never failed—(hear, hear)—whether that object was abroad or whether it wan at Itheir own doom. (Hear, hear.) In this case the appliution was made to the Mayor by the Lord Mayor of Dublin, AS he underetood, to calla meeting of the town to see if Rambling I , could not be done to relieve the distress existing in Ireland, . ' and if they had, as many Cr mosi of them had, calls at home, they still could spare a little to show their sympathy ' with the inhabitants 01 01,0 sister ent as they WAD, in great meaeure upon agriculture and its puducts, and knowing as they did what a disastrous . summer we had had during the year IVO. In fact, if they would forgive him a little Irish bull, he might say the summer of 1870 was nothing but winter. (Laughter ) jThere could be no doubt about it that parts of Ireland were languishing for want of trade. They had not the iron and coal, and the facility of this country, but they were depend- • sot on the products of the soil for theirabsolute maintenance. I They lived in wretched habitations which would not content • the English, and they farml on very ehort commons indeed at all times, but they had not, even to believe the accounts he bad read, Hat small pittance which was necessary to keep : the eoul and may together. They knew the Irishman • whatever lie might be—and sometimes in political matters they had trouble with loim—they knew his faulta were Inever tloose of the heart, though sometimes they might think they procomoled perhaps front lois wroeg headedness. Atoll events, they were never faults ot his heart. He was always ready to give "the bit and the sup" as long as he had it, his hospitality was unbounded, his generosity was , great, and they intiet not forget that in all the battles which ' this country had fought, the Irislunoon had always stoml by I Scotch and English kinsmen, and been reodv 'and willing j whenever milled upon ft support the Queen awl Constitu- , tion. On Thursday last the 15th annual general meeting of , the shareholders connected with the above hank was held I on the bank eternise., Winwick.street, Mr. .1. C. Parr pre. I siding. There were also present—Colonel .1. F. (treenail , (deputy chairmanl, Sir Hilbert ltreenall, Kart., M.F. ca. G. M'Corquodale, Sir A. B. Walker, Sir Thornas li. Frost. Rey. Dr. Carr, Messre. P. Stubs. I Failures had shaken the confidence of the people and j.rm. dared a stagnation in trod, of which no one 0•101.1 tell where it would end. Since last midemniner. how- , ever, there had been a revival in trade, and there was ' now activity where there had but recently been des-1 pondency and uncertainty. tie did not say that it , ' was all over. There were some who thought the revival . would not last. Them still was depression among the agri- 1 cultural connounity, although tne commercial and industrial eenwes were brisker. In the locality in which the hank was situated they did not feel the depreenion as much as did! tiers, though those engaged in agricultural pursuits were not no comfortable as formtrly. The balance sheet, he thought, was one that they ode feel proud of, and that 0.. shareholders would regard,. th more than satisfaction.l They bad since loot veer added £70,000 to the reserve fund, which made it I:249,000. and that made it unnecessary for them to add to it this rear. Whilst witness was on the door he was kick,/ on his back, arms, and ritoo by the three male prisoners. The women were lugging an'd striking him. He got up, and all six pri- soners attacked him and Comm—Francis Charles with a walking-stick with to iron ferrule on, James Charles with a ; miner's rammer, and John Charles with the piece of iron produced. The three female prisoners attacked them with their fists. Witnem got three blows on the arm from the , men with 1,01, Weapon,. He Saw Comm struck on the head by the three rink primnera with their weapons, causing ' blood to flow. He also saw the three women strike Comm with their fists. Ilia twitnem's) shins were bruised by the kicks ; a piece of the skin from the left leg was kicked out, and the ',lnce bled. The cup ethic knee was kicktal, and swollen. He was also struck on his right Wird by Francis Charles with his walking stick : also by Janim Charles, on the same arm with the rammer. That was whilst he was defending himself from the attack. In consequence of what the (primmer@ were .loing, he was completely beaten. aml Francis Charles was rescued:and they were for., cibly put out of the house. He went to Dr. Barrow tino trams day and had his wounds deemed. Comm was much more seri- ously hurt than he was, and he I witness) had to get assist- , mos to take him to the elector.

Joseph Camm said he seasons of the bailiffs of the Leigh County Court. On the 21st January he went to Ocilborne with Ilichwd Wm Carter, to execute a warrant from the Leigh County Court against Fronde Charles. He saw Car- ter go into Charles', house, and followed hint in a few minutes, when hem.. Carter and • woman on the floor. all , the prisoners were there. The prieoner Frannie Charles was striking the last witness with a walking Kick. James Charles was using an iron rammer, and John Charles was using the pleee of iron produced. Bridget Charles wae kicking Carter. Bridget Fairhurst wail also kicking hint, and Mary Braley was standing by. He then tried to assist Carter, when Francis Charles turned on hint (witness), and struck him on Ike right side of the head , with his stick, causinz, a deep Irntald and making it bleed. ! The prisoner Jame. Charles asked him to go out. but he re- fusel. Ile then struck him on the left side of the had with la miner's rammer, making a wonnol in the heed and causing blood to flow, saying. "Take that, you —." The prisoner John Cqarles struck him in the face with his fete. The three female prisoners set on him with their fists. James Charles asked him to go out again, ad he refused. The prisoner John Charles came up with the piece of iron pmcleed. struck : him across the left eye and the face, and gave him a severe I kick on the right foot. The three prisoners then left him and ! went to Carter, but the three female prisoners came and ; kicked and abused him. Carter came to his assistence, and as he was near the door ell the prisoners rushed on him to I put him not. He was knocked down, and they began kick- ing him like • football. He stuck to the door to keep th• prisoner Francis Charles from escaping, and as he was holding the gide of the door Francie struck ' him acmes the back of his hand with his stick ' twice, and he also struck him on the right . side of the face with the same instrument. He alw struck I witness on the shoulders and whereeer he could. Witness I was so dazed and Mimed that he became powerless, and could continue no longer. Ile produced the handkerchief which he used to the wounds to his head. It was stained . with blood, the result of those wounds. His coat, waistcoat, land trousers were also stained with blood. In consequence of the blows inflicted on the wrist he had been unable toner it ; it was eore yet. When he said that he was dazed he meant that he was almost unconscious, and had been laid up from the wounds to his head and hit side. He remembered when he was taken to the chemists* shop, and afterwards 1)r. Barrow came to the chemists' shop to him. The doctor at onee dressed his wound*. and he had been under medical rare from that tirr.ie tm.til the present. . . . .
